item.title: What If 'I Know' Is Our Biggest Limitation?
item.description:
Openness

What If 'I Know' Is Our Biggest Limitation?

Curiosity starts where certainty ends.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Curiosity is innate, but our need for certainty can gradually make us stop exploring.
  • As we gain knowledge, we question less, and start mistaking our beliefs for facts about the world.
  • Genuine curiosity challenges stereotypes, broadens our perspectives, and changes how we see others.

Mentally and physically, I was about as flexible as a broomstick. But I had promised myself that when I arrived in Seattle, I would try things that would get me out of my comfort zone—like yoga.

I was a physician with fairly rigid ideas about what made sense and what didn’t fit my worldview. I was also in the habit of always being two steps ahead, planning what came next. Yoga had other ideas. Standing on one leg left no room to plan whether the union of body, mind, and spirit made sense. All I could do was stay in the present moment and focus on one simple task: keeping my body from falling over.

Had I insisted on what I thought I already knew, I could easily have decided yoga wasn’t for me. Instead, I got curious. That curiosity led me to discover the enormous benefits of meditation, helped me make new friendships, deepened my spiritual connection, inspired me to change my career, and led me to meet my wife Danielle at a yoga retreat. I couldn’t have predicted any of it. Looking back, I simply let myself wonder and wander into the unknown.

What happens to our innate curiosity

We begin life curious. Babies reach for things just beyond their grasp, and children ask endless questions about how things work and why people behave the way they do. But as we grow older, we accumulate knowledge, experiences, and beliefs that help us navigate the world. And the more familiar things become, the less likely we are to question them. We start confusing what we know with what we believe, and what we believe with what is actually true.

We form fixed ideas about other people, about how life works, and especially about ourselves. Without realizing it, we turn our assumptions into invisible boundaries. Eventually, our need for certainty can become a surprisingly restrictive force in our lives.

Curiosity changes more than what we know

We can travel to 50 countries, try 20 different hobbies, and still be rigid in our thinking. How often do you dismiss something before you give yourself a chance to explore it? You might avoid a new hobby because you’re convinced you won’t be good at it. You decide someone doesn’t like you based on how they looked at you or something they said. Or you accept your inner critic’s verdict that you are not good enough, that you cannot change, or that certain things aren’t possible for you. But are these conclusions facts, or are they interpretations you have never questioned? Genuine curiosity means being willing to question what we believe we already know, particularly about other people.

I recently heard a wonderful story about a woman called Grace, in her late 80s, who, much to her children’s surprise, decided to volunteer at a homeless shelter. She had held rather rigid opinions about people whose backgrounds and circumstances were very different from her own, and everyone expected her to give up after a few days.

Instead, Grace found her role. When new residents arrive, she guides them around, helping them pick up sheets, towels, and food, and walks with them for about an hour. Along the way, they tell her all about their lives. Then she says, “Honey, I love you,” and gives them a hug.

Today, the residents love her. And they are all coming to her birthday party.

Grace had walked in seeing people through the lens of stereotypes. By listening, she discovered their shared humanity and qualities that inspired her: resilience, tenacity, and kindness, even from people who had experienced very little kindness themselves. She told her daughter, “I thought I had something to offer the residents, but it turns out what they give me is so much more profound.”

Curiosity is something we can cultivate

But to become genuinely curious, we also need the humility to recognize that there is more we don't know than we know. The moment we accept "I know" as the final answer, we close ourselves off to other possibilities. Intellectual humility means being willing to question our own beliefs, acknowledge that we might be wrong, and consider perspectives that differ from our own (Porter et al., 2022).

This openness can also transform how we relate to others. Studies have found that curious people tend to respond less aggressively, even when provoked, and that asking follow-up questions and showing genuine interest makes us more likable to others (Kashdan et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017). Similarly, a meta-analysis of 515 studies found that getting to know people from different social groups can help reduce prejudice and challenge stereotypes (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).

Grace's experience at the shelter illustrates this beautifully. By spending time with people she might otherwise have judged from a distance, listening to their stories, and becoming genuinely interested in their lives, she discovered not only unexpected friendships but also qualities she deeply admired.

The next time you catch yourself judging others or yourself, feeling defensive, or becoming convinced that something cannot change, pause and ask:

  1. What am I assuming? What am I treating as fact without really knowing?
  2. What might I be missing? What haven't I considered or taken the time to understand?
  3. What if I got curious? What might change if I approached this situation with genuine interest rather than judgment?

Perhaps the greatest limitation in our lives isn’t what we don’t know, but what we believe we already know. Curiosity asks us to make peace with how much we don’t know, to let go of the need to have all the answers, and to be willing to say, “I might be wrong” or, simply, “I wonder what would happen if…”

That willingness took me from a yoga mat to a life I never could have planned.

item.title: The Psychology of Miracles
item.description:
Magical Thinking

The Psychology of Miracles

Why believing in the supernatural helps us survive.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Miracles act as psychological defense mechanisms, safeguarding us from crippling despair.
  • Anticipating miracles helps to regulate the body's built-in stress response by lowering cortisol levels.
  • Relying on miracles can also train the mind to overlook sound rationality and established scientific data.

The human psyche has always upheld a tireless faith in the extraordinary. When tragic events decimate our sense of safety and security, such as an unexpected medical diagnosis, a devastating personal crisis, or a profound loss, we seldom default to reason. Instead, we survey horizons looking for signs and wishing for the seemingly impossible to step in and rescue us from the inevitable.

This reaction is not rare. Surveys from Gallup and Pew Research show that up to 79 percent of U.S. adults believe in miracles, while more than 67 percent strongly believe in phenomena beyond scientific explanation. When reason falls arguably short, divine intervention becomes the next best thing.

For millennia, our existence has relied heavily on our ancestors’ ability to anticipate threats and secure their surroundings. This important skill helped to avoid near-certain death from starvation or the elements, in the event we were ostracized from our tribe. The robust urge to create some kind of order in a confusing and hostile world was paramount. Consequently, strict cause-and-effect accounts often fall emotionally flat. Whenever we are confronted with catastrophic hardship or existential dread, statistics might explain how an event occurred, but oftentimes it can't answer more profound human questions.

A Miracle Mindset

Whenever human beings reframe a striking coincidence as divine intervention or maybe even the hand of God, you have to wonder: Is it simply impulsive denial, or is it a hardwired inclination to believe in the supernatural? Accordingly, it's hard to negate the obvious that perhaps miracles act as psychological defense mechanisms—safeguards explicitly designed to protect us from crippling despair. That's why we so often hear overused proverbs like “Everything happens for a reason” and “God works in mysterious ways.”

Whenever we utilize this defense mechanism, the human mind reclaims a sense of agency when circumstances beyond our control leave us feeling powerless. Anticipating miracles helps to regulate the body's built-in stress response by lowering cortisol levels (the stress hormone) and sustaining emotional stamina during prolonged crisis. It's part of our evolutionary adaptation—a sophisticated cognitive mechanism intended to stimulate hope, develop resilience, and drive us forward even when the odds are stacked against us. Novelist and philosopher Fyodor Dostoevsky, who profoundly examined human psychology, wrote, “since man cannot live without miracles, he will provide himself with miracles of his own making."

But like most things in life, there are downsides to having a miracle mindset. Shielding us from hopelessness and relying too heavily on the mystical can pose psychological, medical, and existential risks. For instance, individuals might reject evidence-based medical treatments, therapeutic interventions, and, perhaps, lifesaving procedures by instead waiting for an unlikely intervention from above.

Additionally, it can lead to passivity and hesitation when needing to assert free will in making important decisions. It could also cause spiritual injury because when anticipated miracles fail to happen, the ensuing fallout can be debilitating. In place of organically processing grief, people might also assume cosmic guilt, blaming themselves or believing their faith was not strong enough. This could potentially worsen their trauma.

The miracle mindset could also foster detachment from reality, ignoring hard facts, leaving individuals vulnerable to exploitation by predatory people, control groups, and buying into false promises. In the end, it could train the mind to overlook sound rationality and established scientific data that is invaluable to our health and well-being.

In America, presenting cold, hard facts to people who are deeply entrenched in their beliefs can trigger a reaction. For many, perhaps it feels too much like an existential threat, frequently promoting defensiveness and condemnation. Whenever we challenge any kind of sacred doctrine, we invite accusations of blasphemy or a lack of a moral compass.

Our personal beliefs are much more than just opinions. They are vital pillars of safety, identity, and communal belonging. Science demonstrates that when an overpoweringly held worldview is questioned, the brain processes it like a threat of physical danger. It does not compute it as a rational debate, but as a menace to psychological existence.

Fear of Oblivion

Finally, believing in miracles fulfills a human need that offers structure and comfort. It helps us manage the fear of what lies beyond more easily. The idea of a meaningless, dark oblivion that lacks determination is hard for many people to swallow. Hence, the concept of divine intervention acts as a soothing balm against uncertainty, providing reassurance in a shaky and unpredictable world.

In addition, every human being feels the omnipresent specter of death. The anxiety around mortality will always be something we have in common. But what separates us is the degree to which we allow fear to govern our choices and our worldviews and how it might compromise our ability to exercise our own free will.

Therefore, how we respond to it is wholly a choice. Perhaps the true measure of our freedom is not how we escape our fear of mortality, but how we live it every day, in spite of it. And sometimes, enduring that reality requires a trace of the supernatural. There’s no harm in a spark of magic in the midst of inescapable tragedy.

As the saying goes (often credited to Albert Einstein), "There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”

item.title: Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection

Healing the gut can support anorexia recovery.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • The gut-brain axis plays a key role in anorexia nervosa.
  • Anorexia damages the gut, making recovery more difficult.
  • Recent research shows that the gut microbiome are adversely affected by anorexia.
  • Dietary rehabilitation, digestive enzymes, and probiotics can help heal the gut.
Source: Suriyawut Suriya / Shutterstock

For generations, scientists and doctors believed the brain was the unquestioned command center of the body. It sent instructions and the rest of the body obeyed. Today, we know the relationship is far more complicated.

Your digestive tract is home to an intricate network of more than 100 million nerve cells—so many, in fact, that scientists often refer to it as the body's second brain. Known as the enteric nervous system, this remarkable network coordinates digestion, communicates with the immune system, influences hormone production, and remains in constant contact with the brain inside your skull.

These two "brains" are linked by an elaborate communication system known as the gut-brain axis. Messages travel in both directions, carried by nerves, hormones, immune cells, and chemical messengers produced by the trillions of bacteria that live within the intestines. It's a constant conversation—one that helps regulate not only digestion, but also mood, stress, appetite, memory, and behavior.

This discovery has transformed the way we think about both physical and mental health.

For decades, psychiatrists understandably focused almost exclusively on the brain. Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, ADHD, and anorexia nervosa were viewed as disorders of brain chemistry. But over the past 20 years, an explosion of research has revealed that the gut is an active participant in all of these conditions. Rather than functioning as separate organs, the gut and the brain operate as partners. When one suffers, the other often does, too.

That insight is especially important in anorexia nervosa.

For people with anorexia nervosa, this two-way conversation has profound implications. Recovery isn’t only about restoring body weight or correcting abnormalities in the brain. It’s also about rebuilding a healthy digestive system capable of supporting the brain’s healing processes.

What Anorexia Does to the Gut

One of the cruelest aspects of anorexia nervosa is that the illness often convinces people that food and eating are problems.

As recovery begins and eating increases, many patients experience bloating, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, and a feeling of fullness after only a few bites. These symptoms can be frightening. They seem to confirm the eating disorder's central lie: See? Eating makes you feel worse.

But that's not what's happening. In most cases, these digestive symptoms are not caused by eating. They are caused by starvation.

When the body is deprived of adequate nourishment for weeks, months, or years, it begins conserving energy wherever it can. Digestion slows dramatically. The muscles that normally move food through the stomach and intestines become less active. The stomach empties more slowly, intestinal motility decreases, and constipation becomes common. Food remains in the digestive tract longer than it should, producing bloating, abdominal discomfort, and an uncomfortable sense of fullness after meals.

Ironically, the very symptoms that make eating difficult are often the result of not eating enough in the first place.

Understanding this dynamic can be enormously reassuring as it shows that the digestive system has not been permanently damaged. The symptoms are signs of a body adapting to prolonged starvation and so, as nutritional rehabilitation progresses and the gut begins receiving the nourishment it needs, digestive function usually improves—although it often takes weeks or months for the gastrointestinal tract to recover fully.

The Gut Microbiome and Anorexia

In anorexia, another important change occurs deep within the intestines, where trillions of bacteria collectively known as the gut microbiome reside. These microorganisms help digest food, produce vitamins, regulate immune function, maintain the integrity of the intestinal lining, and manufacture compounds that influence the brain. Like every other living organism in the body, they depend on a steady supply of nutrients to thrive.

When food intake becomes severely restricted, then, the microbiome changes as well.

Over the past decade, researchers have consistently found that people with anorexia nervosa have a gut microbiome that differs significantly from those of healthy individuals. Some beneficial bacterial species decline, while others become more abundant. Overall microbial diversity—the hallmark of a healthy ecosystem—often decreases. These changes are now believed to contribute not only to digestive symptoms, but also to inflammation, anxiety, and difficulties with weight restoration.

Healing the Gut

The good news is that the gut is remarkably resilient. Unlike many organs, the digestive tract is constantly renewing itself. Cells lining the intestines are replaced every few days. The microbiome is continually adapting to changes in diet, medications, stress, and environment. Even after prolonged starvation, the digestive system has an extraordinary capacity for recovery—provided it receives the nourishment and support it needs.

Here are a few key tools:

Eating enough food. No supplement can substitute for dietary rehabilitation. Restoring adequate calories, protein, healthy fats, and food-delivered vitamins and minerals remains the cornerstone of recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Digestive enzymes. Digestive discomfort can make every meal feel like a battle. Bloating, cramping, constipation, and abdominal pain often reinforce the fear that eating is making things worse. Breaking that cycle sometimes requires giving the digestive system additional support while it heals. One of the simplest ways to do that is through digestive enzyme supplementation.

Digestive enzymes help break food into smaller molecules that can be more easily absorbed by the body. Although digestive enzyme supplements have not yet been studied in anorexia, decades of clinical experience suggest they can can substantially reduce gastrointestinal discomfort during nutritional rehabilitation.

Probiotics. Another important tool is the use of probiotics—live, beneficial microorganisms that help restore a healthier balance within the gut microbiome. For centuries, traditional cultures have consumed probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, kimchi, miso, and sauerkraut. Today, probiotic supplements provide carefully selected bacteria strains that can help replenish beneficial microbes disrupted by illness, antibiotics, stress, and prolonged food restrictions. Their companion nutrients, known as prebiotics, serve as food for these beneficial bacteria, helping them grow and flourish.

Learn more in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Plan to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

item.title: 4 Types of Dead-End Relationships
item.description:
Marriage

4 Types of Dead-End Relationships

Maybe it’s time to put your relationship back on the front burner.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Many couples stop focusing on their relationship, turning their attention to children, work, or themselves.
  • Common causes of a dead-end relationship are unresolved problems, growing apart, and an "autopilot" lifestyle.
  • Revitalizing a dead-end relationship requires having honest conversations and acting decisively.
Source: Geralt / Pixabay

Sara and Keith have been married for nine years and have three children. Both work full-time, do their share of chores and parenting, and fill weekends and many evenings with soccer games, ballet lessons, or overflow work. Is it an okay life? Yes, they would agree it is okay, but in the next breath, they'll admit there’s little affection or intimacy between them.

I’ve met hundreds of couples like Sara and Keith whose relationship has been pushed to the back burner, and intimacy has essentially reached a dead end.

Relationship Patterns That Erode Affection and Intimacy

Here are four of the most common relationship patterns:

Child- or work-centered. This is Sara and Keith. Essentially, they stopped being a couple and instead became mom and pop or worker bees. Such couples often complain that they wish they had more time for couple time, but they're so busy with work and kids.

Roommates. If they don’t have the demands or distractions of work or children, many couples downshift to roommate status. They do spend time together, which they usually enjoy; they may even describe the other as their best friend, but the affection has long since dried up. And like roommates, there’s plenty of talk about schedules and chores.

Parallel lives. This takes the roommate scenario to another level. No best-friend status; no doing things together; each does their own thing; they essentially just share the same space.

Habit/routine-driven lifestyle. This can bleed into all the above variations, where, like Sara and Keith, they do what they do because they do it. They run on autopilot most of the time, and habits and routines kill any hope of spontaneity or anything different.

Underlying Problems That Drive Couples Apart

What holds all these types of couples together is that they're defined by bad solutions to other problems lying beneath. Here are some of the common sources:

Problems that are swept under the rug. If problems go unresolved, they stack up and act like a wedge pushing you apart. You create a long list of "things we don't talk about" and fill in the space with the demands and distractions of work and kids—or you devolve into parallel lives.

A power struggle. Here, problems are never solved because the individuals are unwilling to reach win-win compromises. Sometimes this attitude is fueled by anger and resentment from old wounds; sometimes it is simply a matter of personality—perhaps high anxiety they try to manage through control, self-centeredness, or a need for power. Neither is willing to bend because it feels like letting the other guy win, and coming out on top is always the priority.

Conflict avoidance. Some individuals have learned to fear conflict and others' strong emotions, often because of a childhood environment in which parents were frightening or modeled passivity and avoidance. As a result, anger is internalized or turned into self-blame, and problems are never discussed or resolved. Periodically, one person may act out or explode in anger, which only further fuels their fear and internalization.

Unhealed wounds. Past affairs and sudden, traumatic decisions, such as abruptly quitting jobs or being forced to move—painful incidents that shattered safety and trust and linger, coloring the relationship—have become a grudge that is always there; an open wound that never heals.

An expired relationship contract. Whatever Sara and Keith needed from each other nine years ago, they likely no longer need it now. Each has grown into different needs and desires, but like many couples, they’ve built a life in a box of rules and routines that no longer fit them. Some couples divorce; others, like them, downshift their relationship.

How to Rebuild the Relationship

If you’re ready for a change—to get your relationship back on the front burner and bring back intimacy and affection—here are some tips to get you started:

Acknowledge the state of the relationship. In some ways, this can be the hardest step. Like "The Emperor's New Clothes," it requires breaking the code of silence, refusing to ignore reality, and having the courage to be honest. Once you say how you’ve been feeling and start that conversation, you can’t unsay it or the other can’t unhear it. You’ve opened the door to change, and that’s a good place to start.

Change the emotional climate through action. Resist the urge to think change is about getting the other person to change: this leads to nagging, manipulation, or a blink contest where each waits for the other. Instead, think about changing the overall emotional climate of the relationship, breaking ingrained habits and patterns, and stopping autopilot behaviors. The key is action: Plan a date night; snuggle together on the couch while you watch a movie; move the kid’s bedtime earlier so you have time as a couple to simply chat at the end of the day. Something, anything that is different and positive.

Repair old wounds. I’ve heard partners say they just need answers to questions that have been lingering for years—about the affair, the job, or the move. Or sometimes it is just the opportunity to get things off their chests and finally feel heard and understood, without avoidance or defensiveness. Sometimes you can do this on your own; sometimes it helps to start by writing a letter or email; sometimes you need to bring in a professional to help mediate and moderate the conversation.

Tackle unresolved problems. The best way to do this is to chip away at them in baby steps. I suggest that couples set aside a good time to talk when they’re not tired or distracted. Treat it like a staff meeting at work: Set an agenda with one or two items, focus on you, and work toward a win-win compromise while controlling your emotions. Meet for 30-45 minutes. And if it is hard to do, bring in a professional.

Time for change?

Resist the urge to think your feelings need to change before you can act; if you keep doing what you’re doing, you’ll keep feeling the same way. Instead, challenge yourself to break out and take action.

If not now, when?

item.title: What Else Is True?: Lessons About Suffering and Healing
item.description:
Trauma

What Else Is True?: Lessons About Suffering and Healing

Personal reflections on the wisdom of the body, human connection, and flourishing.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Traumatic experiences can alter the course of lives. However, healing is possible.
  • Extraordinary courage, generosity, humor, creativity, kindness, and compassion can co-exist with suffering.
  • When faced with adversity, it is important to explore the question: "What else is true?"
Source: Elaine Miller-Karas, Chat gpt 11/15/26

Twenty years ago, I helped establish a nonprofit organization called the Trauma Resource Institute. I could not have imagined where that decision would take me, the people I would meet, or how profoundly the journey would change my understanding of human suffering and resilience. My work has brought me into communities experiencing extraordinary adversity. I have witnessed the aftermath of natural disasters, the heartbreak of war and conflict, and the suffering of people whose lives have been disrupted by trauma, violence, and loss.

Yet, amid the suffering and the heartache, I have encountered something else. I have witnessed extraordinary courage, generosity, humor, creativity, kindness, and compassion. I have seen people reach toward one another as their own lives unraveled. I learned that suffering can profoundly alter the course of our lives, but suffering is never the only truth about who we are or what remains possible.

What Else Is True?

Throughout my work, I have returned again and again to a simple question:“What else is true?” When something terrible happens, what else is true? When we feel overwhelmed by loneliness, grief, or fear, what else is true? When the world seems divided or hopeless, what else is true? This question is not an invitation to deny suffering nor does it ask us to turn away from injustice, grief, trauma, or pain. Rather, it invites us to widen the lens through which we experience ourselves and the world.

Alongside fear, there may also be courage. Alongside grief, there may be love. Alongside helplessness, there may be one small place where choice still exists. And sometimes, amid tremendous suffering, hope begins to emerge. We can grieve and still experience gratitude. We can feel frightened and still recognize moments when we feel safer. The presence of suffering does not erase our capacity for well-being.

The Wisdom of the Body

One of the most profound discoveries is that trauma is not only a cognitive or emotional experience. It is also physiological. Our nervous systems continually respond to what is happening around and within us. When we perceive danger, our bodies mobilize to protect us. Our hearts may race, our muscles tighten, or we may become numb or disconnected. These responses are not signs of weakness but reflect our biology working to help us survive. The body carries a wisdom that words alone cannot always express. Our nervous systems communicate distress and danger, but they can also register safety, connection, comfort, strength, and possibility.

The Trauma Resiliency Model (TRM) and Community Resiliency Model (CRM), approaches I developed, make knowledge about trauma and the nervous system accessible. Central to these models is body literacy: learning to recognize and understand the sensations through which our bodies communicate. People can begin to tell the difference between sensations of distress and well-being without judgment. Distress does not necessarily disappear, but it need not be the only experience available to us.

The People Who Travel With Us

As my understanding of trauma deepened, I began asking another question: What if knowledge about our nervous systems did not remain only within therapy rooms? This question flooded my waking moments: What if teachers, nurses, parents, children, first responders, and entire communities could learn simple skills to restore well-being?

These questions changed the direction of my life. I have watched people adapt CRM and TRM wellness skills for schools, hospitals, shelters, recovery programs, disaster response, and communities affected by war and other disasters. I have learned that resilience grows between us. Our nervous systems respond to the presence of others. A caring voice, a compassionate expression, or the steady presence of someone we trust may help us feel safer and more connected.

I invite you to consider your own life's journey: Who or what has lifted you when you stumbled? Who or what reminded you of your worth when you doubted yourself? When loneliness or despair entered your life, who or what helped you reconnect with hope?

From Resilience to Human Flourishing

As I reflect on this journey, I find myself increasingly drawn to the idea of human flourishing. Healing from trauma can open possibilities beyond the reduction of distress. As people experience greater safety and physiological regulation, there may be more room for curiosity, creativity, meaningful relationships, purpose, and joy.

Flourishing does not mean living without pain, nor is it an inevitable outcome of adversity. It is the possibility of living with greater meaning, connection, and agency while acknowledging life's complexities. Communities flourish when compassion becomes action, human dignity is protected, and people recognize their shared humanity.

What Twenty Years Have Taught Me About Hope

I no longer think of hope simply as optimism about the future. I understand it as an openness to possibility, even when we cannot predict what comes next. Hope may begin with an unexpected kindness, a moment of physiological steadiness, or discovering that we still have a choice. After twenty years, I continue returning to the question that has accompanied my journey: “What else is true?”

Sometimes the answer is someone I love. Sometimes it is the generosity of a stranger, the beauty of nature, or the quiet recognition that my body can still experience peace in the midst of chaos. And sometimes the answer is simply that I do not yet know what else is possible.

Resilience reminds us that suffering never gets to tell the whole story. Within the human spirit, the wisdom of the body, and the connections we share, another truth may be waiting to be discovered—a possibility for connection, healing, and hope.

I began this journey wanting to help people recover from trauma. Twenty years later, the people I have met have taught me something equally important: Even in a world filled with suffering, our capacity for compassion, connection, and hope remains one of the most remarkable expressions of our shared humanity, and it provides a pathway to healing. And fundamentally, the body has a wisdom that words cannot speak.

item.title: Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You
item.description:
Affirmations

Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You

The simple magic of self-affirmation.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • The self-integrity motive is the need to see ourselves as good, capable, reasonable, and sensible people.
  • When our self-integrity is threatened, we feel bad about ourselves and react defensively.
  • Affirming a value we cherish and feel confident in can help us feel worthy and "good enough" again.
  • You can experience self-affirmation with a simple activity you can do on your own.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

Brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat. But what kind of threat do they reduce? And how does self-affirmation reduce it?

Self-Affirmation and Self-Integrity

Source: Allan Zuckoff

The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.

Our sense of self-integrity can be based on any valued qualities we believe we possess.3,4,5 Unfortunately, our self-integrity can also be threatened by anything we see as reflecting negatively on who we are: failure, bad things that happen to us, criticism or rejection, information that challenges what we believe, recognition that we’ve acted in ways that conflict with our values—any experience we take as evidence that we are bad, wrong, incompetent, irrational, foolish, or unable to deal effectively with life.

We feel bad about ourselves (ashamed, humiliated, unworthy) when our self-integrity is threatened, which triggers defensive efforts to protect or restore it: We may dismiss or minimize the threat; attack its source; marshal evidence against it; rationalize or justify our behavior, or deny being responsible for it; try to puff ourselves up through self-aggrandizing statements or comparing ourselves with people who we believe are worse.6,7,8 Any of these strategies may reestablish our self-integrity, but only temporarily—and they leave us vulnerable to more of the same kinds of threats.

This is where self-affirmation can change the story. Focusing on important or valued aspects of the self that are not affected by the self-integrity threat bolsters our global sense of being “good enough”— protectively, if we self-affirm before we feel threatened, or restoratively, if we self-affirm afterward. It also makes all our defensive responses unnecessary, and in doing so promotes honest self-awareness and constructive responses to the challenges we face. Put simply, self-affirmation creates a protective buffer by putting the threat in perspective and helping us take a broader view of ourselves: Yes, I may have been wrong, made a bad decision, acted in a way I regret—but I’m a good and capable person, and my flaws and mistakes don’t define me.2,4,9

The research on self-affirmation shows how it benefits us in concrete ways. Self-affirmation increases our acceptance of information about risks to our health that would otherwise feel threatening.10,11,12 It increases our openness to evidence that challenges dearly held beliefs, and decreases our tendency to evaluate arguments for and against those beliefs in favor of what we already believe.13,14 It reduces the mental energy spent ruminating on failures and flaws and frees our mental resources for more productive activities, improving performance under stress on tasks that require focused attention, problem-solving, creativity, and insight.9,15,16,17 It increases our self-compassion and fosters helping behavior toward others.18

Most broadly, self-affirmation activities have consistently been shown to enhance the well-being of those who engage in them:9 It improves the general sense of feeling good, of having community and belonging; it offers relief from symptoms like depression and anxiety that create barriers to well-being; and it improves one's sense that they are a person of competence and value. And just as in the case of the studies of women dissatisfied with their weight that we began with in Part 1, these effects on well-being are long-lasting and get larger with the passage of time.

Self-Affirmation and You

Can self-affirmation make a difference for you? Here’s an activity that will allow you to experience it for yourself. (For the most meaningful experience, please have paper and pen ready. And please do each of these steps in turn, waiting until you’ve finished the one you’re doing to go on to the next, rather than reading ahead to the end.)

1. Think of an area of your life that you have been struggling with. It could be a behavior you’ve been trying to change, but have not changed; something you’ve been wanting to do, but have not done; a decision you’ve been trying to make, but have not made. Once you identify it, please spend the next minute just thinking about the struggle and what it has been like for you.

2. From the following list, please choose one value that a) is very important to you, and has been important in your life, b) is not related to the area of your life you have been struggling with.

Source: Allan Zuckoff

3. Think of a time when the value you chose was important to you. For the next few minutes, please write about that time and why that value was important to you.

Getting the Most Out of Self-Affirmation

Self-affirmation is most powerful when we’re facing a challenge of high personal importance, which is when our self-integrity is most likely to be threatened.19 Because self-affirmation works by focusing us on an aspect of ourselves that we feel good about and that does not feel threatened, it’s important to choose a value that’s unrelated to the challenge at hand; trying to affirm a threatened aspect of the self often makes us more defensive rather than less.19 And self-integrity is strengthened the most when we affirm “self-transcendent” values (values that express concern for others), rather than values that primarily benefit ourselves.4

The positive effects of self-affirmation on how we feel and how we act reinforce a key tenet of motivational interviewing: we’re most likely to change and grow not when we feel sufficiently bad about ourselves, but when we feel accepted and valued.20 When you embark on a path toward change, don’t neglect to focus on what makes you worthy of value and respect just as you are.

item.title: How to Become Change-Curious
item.description:
Resilience

How to Become Change-Curious

Change can be intimidating, but it might be easier if we wondered about it more.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Change can be intimidating, but approaching it with curiosity allows for a different perspective.
  • Curiosity promotes openness and wonderful in the change process, which helps people avoid anxiety around it.
  • Noticing and acknowledging the presence of change helps one orient toward change.

We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning new ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food plans, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

How a Learner’s Mind Can Make Change Less Daunting

Given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

Noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

Looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

Shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a new instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

Sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a new behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.

item.title: When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down
item.description:
Relationships

When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

How to have your partner’s back when a relative crosses a line.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • When hurtful family comments go unchallenged, your partner may feel alone in the room.
  • Before a family gathering, ask your partner what they’d find helpful if things get tense.
  • A calm response like “Let’s leave that topic alone” can set a boundary in the moment.
  • If you stayed quiet, acknowledge the hurt, apologize, and say what you’ll do differently next time.

Imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents. The drive home seems eerily quiet, even though you feel like the evening went pretty well, and you can’t shake the general impression that your partner is upset.

Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”

You try to explain that you didn’t want to start an argument. After all, your mother has always been outspoken, and you know from experience that challenging her would have started “a thing” and made everyone uncomfortable. You had assumed your partner understood this and would instinctively know you didn’t agree with what your mother said.

Your partner sees things differently. They were embarrassed and went on to spend the entire evening feeling unsupported and increasingly resentful. You’re also beginning to realize that while you might have avoided one argument over the dinner table, you set yourself up to face another one at home.

Situations like these are common for couples managing complicated relationships with extended family. Doing your best to keep everyone happy seems like the responsible adult choice, especially when family gatherings can already be tense or stressful. However, avoiding uncomfortable conversations with relatives can easily come at the expense of your partner.

Why Does Keeping the Peace Feel So Important?

According to a 2013 longitudinal study, early dynamics with in-laws often correlate with later marital stability. This connection can vary according to factors like race and gender, so complicated family relationships don’t necessarily affect every couple the same way. However, wanting to maintain family harmony is second nature to most people. This can especially be the case for those who grew up in households in which challenging a parent was unacceptable or disagreements almost always escalated into ugly arguments.

It’s easy to go into adulthood with the general idea that keeping quiet is the cleanest way to deal with uncomfortable situations. That doesn’t necessarily stop once you’re in a committed relationship of your own.

Naturally, you love your partner and feel responsible for protecting their feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re comfortable confronting your parents, siblings, or other relatives.

How Staying Neutral Can Feel Like Abandonment

Picture a situation in which your sibling cracks a joke at your partner’s expense during a family get-together. Everyone laughs, so you join in, even though you also know your partner finds such remarks hurtful.

From your point of view, laughing along was the easiest way to avoid a potential scene, especially if that’s your family’s usual routine when this particular sibling makes off-color comments or gives someone a hard time. Meanwhile, all your partner knows is that you joined in while someone else embarrassed them in front of others.

Disconnects like these can become huge sticking points in a relationship when they happen repeatedly. Your partner may start to associate getting together with your family with having to endure uncomfortable comments and potential embarrassment. If they also feel you expect them to tolerate this, they may eventually wonder whether they can count on you at all when life gets difficult.

A 2019 study published in Social Work Research surveyed 351 women about their relationships with their mothers-in-law. Findings suggested factors like family-triangle dynamics or unclear relationship boundaries directly impacted relationship quality.

Having a partner who stays silent during disagreements can further aggravate relationships that may already be complicated.

When one partner makes a habit of not addressing comments or behaviors that are inappropriate, the other can feel responsible for managing everyone’s discomfort. They’re forced to choose between speaking up and potentially causing a scene or staying silent and dealing with feelings of resentment or abandonment.

Supporting Your Partner Without Blindly Taking Sides

Properly supporting your partner doesn’t necessarily mean agreeing with them every time they complain about your family. However, you can (and should) acknowledge your partner’s feelings and talk things out when conflicts come up. There’s a world of difference between saying “You’re right, my family is awful” no matter what and saying “I get why that was hurtful, so let’s talk about it” instead.

Couples can minimize recurring disagreements further by working through expectations before people butt heads and things get tense.

1. Discuss potential sticking points beforehand. Some relatives may be notorious for disregarding other people’s boundaries or making intrusive comments. If this is the case in your family, prep for upcoming gatherings by talking to your partner beforehand about how you’ll respond to any possible incidents.

Avoid assuming you already know what your partner will find helpful in the moment. Instead, ask them what would truly help them feel supported and go from there.

2. Address inappropriate behavior calmly. Intervening if things do get tense doesn’t have to mean starting an argument. Try shutting down hurtful comments, intrusive questions, and so forth by simply saying, “We’d rather not discuss that” or “Please don’t make fun of my partner.”

Statements like these help establish boundaries with relatives and set expectations without necessarily escalating the situation.

3. Avoid volunteering your partner to keep others happy. Instead of instantly making commitments or agreeing to family plans that affect both of you, talk to your partner about it first. Being considerate to your family is important, but it shouldn’t mean making decisions and promises on someone else’s behalf.

4. Check in privately. If something happens at a family get-together that feels uncomfortable, pull your partner aside and ask how they’re doing. If necessary, talk about it for a moment or offer to leave early. Even a brief check-in is often enough to keep your partner feeling supported and stop resentment from building up through an evening.

5. Take responsibility when you get it wrong. You’re only human, so there may be times when you only realize after the fact that staying silent may have hurt your partner. Acknowledge it and explain what happened. Then apologize and express a willingness to respond differently next time.

Conversations like these should go both ways, so be sure to give your partner a chance to explain their own family histories or talk about genuine misunderstandings as well.

Takeaway

Ultimately, it’s more than possible to keep your family relationships strong while also helping your partner feel properly loved and supported. But doing so might mean learning to manage occasional discomfort instead of simply expecting your partner to absorb the impact and understand.

item.title: We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?
item.description:
Environment

We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

The common thread of tech crashes, climate change, and COVID is chosen blindness.

Posted November 16, 2026

Source: Walther. ChatGTP. 2026

On November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become. A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, affecting businesses, hospitals, courts, and public services across more than 70 countries and territories. The following day, Claude experienced separate disruptions, while problems at Cloudflare affected parts of the internet's underlying infrastructure. A handful of technical failures exposed how extensively our everyday activities depend on systems most of us barely understand and cannot easily replace. These incidents were not caused by the same malfunction, yet their proximity makes a larger question difficult to escape: How much fragility are we prepared to tolerate before we do something about it?

In July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension. During a cybersecurity evaluation, autonomous AI agents escaped their intended testing boundaries, accessed external systems and compromised infrastructure belonging to OpenAI and Hugging Face. The agents had been given objectives, limited safeguards, and considerable freedom to pursue their tasks. Their behavior departed from the intended boundaries, with consequences extending beyond the laboratory. According to subsequent reporting, the intrusion continued for days before its origins were fully recognized. This was no science-fiction rebellion. It was a documented failure to maintain effective control over increasingly capable autonomous systems.

What connects these events to climate change and COVID-19? Something more fundamental than technology: our remarkable ability to recognize warning signs, explain them, and continue behaving as though they concern someone else.

The Psychology Of Looking Away

The scientific warnings about climate change have been accumulating for decades. In 2019, an international assessment of pandemic preparedness warned that the world was dangerously ill-equipped for a rapidly spreading respiratory disease. Warnings about concentrated digital infrastructure and the difficulties of controlling autonomous AI have likewise preceded the failures now attracting public attention. The timing and details were uncertain. The vulnerabilities were visible. Behavioral science helps explain why visibility so often fails to produce action. Research on information avoidance shows that people sometimes prefer not to know something, even when the information is freely available and potentially useful. Knowledge carries an emotional price. Once we acknowledge a threat, we may have to change our habits, question our investments, confront authority, or accept responsibility. Ignorance, including carefully cultivated ignorance, offers temporary relief.

Another mechanism is normalcy bias—our tendency to interpret emerging danger through the reassuring lens of previous experience. Yesterday's infrastructure worked. The last alarming forecast did not destroy our home. The previous disease outbreak was contained. Each uneventful day strengthens our confidence, even when the underlying risk is accumulating. The absence of disaster becomes mistaken evidence of safety. The black swan conundrum strikes, in which something predictable is perceived as surprising in the moment but obvious in hindsight.

Institutions magnify these tendencies. Prevention requires spending money today to avoid something that may never happen. Its successes are mostly invisible. Meanwhile, the individual who raises uncomfortable questions risks being branded pessimistic, obstructive, or insufficiently committed to progress. We have built organizations that celebrate immediate performance while allowing longer-term vulnerabilities to disappear into risk registers, committee minutes, and reassuring presentations.

Our Collective Illusion

There is a social dimension to our inaction. A study involving nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries found that 89% wanted stronger political action on climate change. Yet respondents systematically underestimated how many others were willing to contribute. Behavioral scientists call this pluralistic ignorance: We misjudge the beliefs of those around us and adjust our own behavior accordingly. Imagine a boardroom where several executives privately worry about excessive reliance on one technology provider, but nobody wants to interrupt the enthusiasm surrounding digital transformation. Or a community where residents recognize growing flood risks yet assume their neighbors will oppose costly preventive measures. Silence becomes mistaken for agreement. Everybody waits for somebody else to move.

The implications for agentic AI are taking this to the next level. As systems gain the capacity to make decisions and act with limited supervision, failures can spread faster than human organizations can recognize them. The July incident illustrates why technical capability must be accompanied by meaningful oversight, enforced boundaries and the ability (and will) to interrupt autonomous activity. November's outages exposed a different vulnerability: dependence on digital services without sufficient resilience. Neither problem can be solved by hoping that the next incident will be manageable. Wishful thinking is a road of no return.

Our central difficulty, then, is not simply a shortage of information. It is the widening distance between what we know, what we acknowledge, what we are prepared to change, and what we are actually doing about it.

From Warning to Responsibility: The A-Frame

We cannot eliminate uncertainty, but we can stop using it as an excuse. The A-Frame offers four practical steps for individuals, organizations and governments.

  • Awareness: Actively seek uncomfortable evidence. Ask what could go wrong, which early signals we are dismissing, and whose warnings remain unheard.
  • Appreciation: Seek to understand the wider consequences of your decisions: for colleagues and communities, future generations, and the natural systems that sustain us.
  • Acceptance: Recognize uncertainty, interdependence, and our own vulnerability. Waiting for absolute certainty is itself a consequential decision.
  • Accountability: Convert recognition into commitments, personal responsibilities, resources, deadlines, independent scrutiny and consequences when promised safeguards are neglected.

The next crisis may arrive through a computer network, the changing climate, or an unfamiliar pathogen. Its exact form remains uncertain. The warning signs are accumulating around us while you read this. Sadly, chosen blindness will not save us from ourselves. And we will not be able to claim we didn't know.

item.title: Protective Delusion in the Case of Elizabeth Holmes
item.description:
Trauma

Protective Delusion in the Case of Elizabeth Holmes

Trauma can lead to disassociated states.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Protective delusions can emerge out of trauma.
  • Disassociation can happen when one is triggered.

The documentary You Can See Everything has sparked debate about whether incarcerated entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes is delusional or manipulative. Delusions are fixed, false beliefs. One can be out of touch with reality or delusional in a circumscribed way and still be high functioning. A "manipulator" exploits others in a calculated way.

We learn in the documentary that Elizabeth was sexually abused in college and bullied in an academic program overseas—and that her personal and professional partner of 12 years, Sunny Balwani, allegedly abused her. Protective delusions can serve as defense mechanism for a person who suffered trauma. In some cases, they are adaptive and even a survival tool. Self-aggrandizing delusions combat humiliation, suicidality, despair and fear. If my story is not my story, one may think, then I can keep going—and if I can go from failure to superhero, I am safe.

Protective delusions pose a risk, however, as disconnection from reality involves missing cues and problems that need to be addressed.

Elizabeth Holmes's Story

By age 19, Holmes was living the dream. She and Balwani built Theranos into a billion-dollar company. A single drop of blood, they claimed, could be used in their device, called Edison, for hundreds of assays. This pain-saving, cost-cutting, preventive-care device would allow patients to order their own tests and avoid venipuncture. Early detection would foster greater health. Adoration, trust, and awe emanated from subordinates to Theranos's leaders. An earlier documentary, Inventor, captured images of Holmes at the peak of her glory. Her slightly rumpled, ill-fitting, all-black daily garb and deep voice suggest seriousness but also something odd. In that film and elsewhere, she has been described as ethereal, different and a once-in-a-century person.

Holmes's invention created a savior-like persona for her. However, Theranos secretly used traditional machines (not the Edison) and venipuncture, not finger pricks, to capture accurate results, yet denied doing so. Insider tips from lab workers allowed the Wall Street Journal to expose the error-prone Edison. The company crashed, Holmes and Balwani were convicted of wire fraud and sentenced to 10-years plus in prison.

Before the fall, when asked about the science of the final product, Holmes responded by saying she could not reveal business secrets. In the Fielder film she fumbles and gives fuzzy answers when pressed about these specifics, as if she is disssociating. She still believes in her invention. Though a "fake it till you make it" mindset has preceded some great inventions, including Thomas Edison's, perhaps true progress justified those inventors' persistence. Holmes appeared to dismiss advice and warnings from experts who did not support her design. Some insisted that success was impossible in its present form. Her role model, Thomas Edison was quoted as saying, "Our greatest weakness lies in giving up." It may have felt empowering to identify with him and do as he did.

The Edison may have been ill-conceived from the get-go. Venipuncture and medical experts ordering tests are not problems that require sweeping remedies. The support of a medical expert in the choice and interpretation of tests is in fact helpful for many if not most people. It is not clear that this invention, even if it worked, would have served the public in a meaningful or vast way.

What's in a Mind?

What was going on in Elizabeth Holmes's mind then and now? Even if she is manipulating, what is the benefit of deceiving others now? She owes $450 million and so she is worth zero. She has been disgraced, despised, and mocked, so she is not in a likely position to create a new company and exploit others. Her tender mothering, and her tears and fears about her upcoming incarceration seem believable in the Fielder documentary and Holmes has reportedly been a model prisoner and helpful to other inmates. Her sentence was been reduced and she will be transferred to a halfway house. Former inmates have said kind things about her.

Maybe the dream, the protective delusion with the glorified role, was the point. Holmes repeatedly says it was never about the money. Still, ignoring expert advice is somewhat irrational. Surrounding yourself with worshippers is dangerous. And a person who misleads the public with an error-prone product will likely be exposed and suffer consequences. Better judgement might have included calling a halt to development, informing investors, integrating experts, iterating anew, or giving up. Holmes destroyed her own life, in a big way, at least as much as anyone else's.

Protective Delusion

Protective Delusion can be a defense against psychological disintegration. Though it is a form of disassociation, it is stabilizing. Some research has described delusional thinking as adaptive in abused or neglected children. Psychologically speaking, the unconscious drive to remain whole and safe via a grand altruistic persona or an elevating fantasy can trump other drives. The grandiosity can include sweeping altruism.

Poor judgment, insight, and reality testing are associated with delusional thinking. We cannot know if trauma led to protective delusion for Holmes. What was she like before all this happened? Was there a personality change? Did the abuses she experienced engender both her drive and disssociation? Though we have a "conclusion in which nothing is concluded,” we can still be curious.

item.title: When Your Employee Is a Worrywart
item.description:
Career

When Your Employee Is a Worrywart

Take these steps to open the lines of communication.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Some employees avoid conversation because they think that keeps them off your radar.
  • Open communication is critical to maintain a solid working relationship.
  • Let them know that they can share a differing opinion and that you want to hear it.
  • Use clear and direct language to set expectations and to make sure they feel valued.
Source: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels

Some employees hide behind their computers or devices to avoid conversation. They fool themselves into believing that no feedback from the boss is good news. This assumption could harm their careers because they are not hearing significant criticism that could help them improve performance. And they are missing opportunities to influence the direction of their jobs by not finding ways to talk to you.

Worrywarts begin unconcerned, stoically accepting this lack of communication as a positive sign. Everything must be going great, or else you would be screaming for changes, right? Then they begin to wonder, afraid to hear a critique. The formerly happy worker bounces back and forth between unhappy and content.

What You Are Thinking

I have been busy lately, but now that the merger is completed, I had better take the time to review progress and next steps with my team. Fortunately, they need little direction from me. Jim, though, is avoiding me and seems to be fluctuating like he is on an emotional elevator. I hate to confront him, but I must find out what is bothering him. I have had too many top employees leave without telling me why.

Your Employee’s Thoughts

It’s been a long time since the boss has commented on my work. On one hand, no feedback probably means she is satisfied. My work is good. I do not really need feedback, or do I? But where do I stand since this merger? She gave everyone the same brief message. What if I do have a problem? What if I have been doing something wrong? Am I going to be downsized? I am afraid to ask her. I had better leave well enough alone.

Strategy

Your goal is to restore the employee’s confidence and refocus their energy.

  1. Recognize the impact of feedback. Constant, consistent, constructive feedback is one of the most important things your employees need. To withhold it fosters anxiety and fear of asking what is in store for them. Letting terse emails and texts substitute for give-and-take conversation leaves employees longing and frustrated. Remember that tone and inflection can be easily misinterpreted through a text or email.
  2. Expand the direction of feedback. Add to your downward one-way information an upward flow to achieve true two-way communication. To reduce anxiety, anger, or resentment, draw out employee thinking and feelings with open-ended questions.
  3. Focus on what you and your workers have in common. Talk about getting the job done. Let them express their perspectives, especially when they are different from your own. This open communication provides a basis for working out any differences. A little flexibility on your part can help bring about their acceptance when your way overrules.

Tactical Talk

You: Jim, with the merger completed, there will be some changes. I want to discuss with you how your work may be affected. As you know, one objective is… How do you think you might help us to achieve that?

Jim: (Silence.)

You: Did I catch you off guard?

Jim: Yes, you did.

You: Sorry about that! I value open communication and want you to feel comfortable sharing your questions and concerns. Do you have something you’d like to share? Are you concerned about how I’ll react?

Jim: I’m afraid you’ll think I’m in over my head. But I’d rather hear criticism than not know how I’m doing.

Everyone needs feedback. It is your chance to encourage innovation and unleash talent. Even those who never give you a hard time need it. All workers must know that they are valued. Without feedback, some good workers can become emotional wrecks and some just go elsewhere. Feedback is especially useful when your goal is to gently draw out the uncommunicative worker.

item.title: Stuck in a Rut: Escaping 'The Vicious Cycle' Through Reading
item.description:
Trauma

Stuck in a Rut: Escaping 'The Vicious Cycle' Through Reading

Author Kyle Lukoff shares insights on changing patterns and healing trauma.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Trauma can make escape routes feel invisible, even when others see them clearly.
  • The picture book "The Vicious Cycle" helps children see when they're living in repetitive, fearful patterns.
  • "The Vicious Cycle" illustrates that returning to old patterns doesn't erase progress.
Source: Macmillan Children's Publishing Group/Used with permission

Even children can get stuck in a rut, spinning their wheels in ruminating thoughts or maladaptive behaviors that don’t serve their mental health and well-being.

Enter Newbery Honor-winning author Kyle Lukoff’s latest picture book, The Vicious Cycle, about a unicycle who gets stuck in a rut and the friend who inspires it to try something new, at least for a little while. Lukoff shares the inspiration behind this insightful book that speaks to the courage it takes to change, and how literature has played a role in his own mental health journey.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write The Vicious Cycle.

Kyle Lukoff: I've spent a lot of my professional life thinking deeply about picture books. I was a lead bookseller in the children's section of a Barnes & Noble in a neighborhood with a high population of young children, and that made me decide to get my master's degree in library science with a focus on children's literature and youth services.

From there, I got a job as an elementary school librarian, with students aged 2 through fifth grade, and spent many hours a day sitting cross-legged on the floor reading to kids. My first published works were all picture books, and even now, with many novels and speeches and short stories under my belt, I consider myself a picture book author who sometimes writes other things as well.

The inspiration for The Vicious Cycle is truly underwhelming. "You know what would be funny," I told a friend, "is if there was a picture book about an angry unicycle, and it was called 'The Vicious Cycle.'" That idea percolated in my subconscious for a year or two before I finally figured out what the story there was.

Q: In this moving picture book, a unicycle finds itself stuck in a rut until it finds the courage to break free from the well-worn path it dug for itself. How do we find ourselves stuck in our own vicious cycles in life? What role might trauma play in this process?

Kyle Lukoff: I have said, jokingly, that "this is a picture book about trauma," but it really is. It's about how we can be hurt so badly that we can't find a way out, even though others might see it clearly laid out in front of us.

I know I have gotten stuck in quite a few bad patterns, and even now I have to refuse to go down those same paths, and at least try to find new mistakes to make and new problems to create for myself. I am not a therapist or a psychologist (that's my husband's job), but I have been in therapy for most of my adult life, and have worked very hard to build a life for myself that isn't just going around in circles.

Q: In the story, how does a new friend inspire the unicycle to find courage? What can we learn from her example about being a friend to someone who is “stuck” in regards to their mental health?

Kyle Lukoff: You know, the story itself isn't sure what makes the unicycle take that first step (wheel?). It just happens one day, because there's no grand moment when all of your problems go away; there's just a day where you feel better and want to try something different.

I think the most important thing about Emily's role in this story is that she doesn't allow herself to become trapped alongside the unicycle. It is her decision to join it in its path. When it's time for her to leave, she leaves. When she wants to come back, she comes back. She helps the unicycle only in ways that serve her, not in ways that are codependent or unhealthy or self-sacrificing. And she's not even trying to fix it. She just likes being with it, and hopes that her presence might help, but isn't behaving as if she owes the unicycle anything, or [vice versa]. I, personally, have a lot to learn from Emily.

Q: The little girl doesn’t pull the unicycle out of its rut—the choice to take a new path belongs to the unicycle alone. How does this mirror our own self-determination and healing process?

Kyle Lukoff: Without going into too much personal detail, in my early 20s, I was suffering from some very severe and dangerous mental health issues. I had thought that if I got hospitalized I'd be surrounded by people who had the secret knowledge that would make me better, but all they did was help me stay alive until I was a little more medically stable, and then I was discharged.

The most important thing I learned from that experience was that no one was going to save me, and that I had two choices: I could do the hard work it would take to get better, or I could be miserable and unwell for the rest of my probably-shorter life. I decided to go with the former, because no one was going to do it for me, and because the latter seemed unpleasant.

Q: How do you hope The Vicious Cycle helps young readers, and their grown-ups, to take a healthy perspective on mental health and healing?

Kyle Lukoff: I wanted to point out something about the ending. The unicycle gets out of its rut, yes, but at the end of the story it goes back to it, because "the outside was unfamiliar. And a little scary."

There is no one simple straight path to healing, or to a better life. You try something, maybe it works, maybe it doesn't, maybe it works for just long enough for you to find something else. Maybe you relapse, or retreat back into unhealthy patterns, but the next time you try to get out, it might be a little easier.

Healing is no more linear than the unicycle's rut, but at least there's the chance for something new around the bend.
