item.title: How to Explain Adoption to a Child
item.description:
Adoption

How to Explain Adoption to a Child

Every adoption carries a responsibility to help children understand their story.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Children need to hear their adoption story early and repeatedly, because understanding changes as they grow.
  • Honest explanations, compassionate language, and permission to ask questions help children.
  • Silence about adoption can contribute to confusion, self-blame, and feelings of rejection.

November is National Adoption Month, a time when we celebrate families formed through adoption and acknowledge there are children who still need safe, loving, permanent homes. Yet adoption is more than the creation of a new family. It also involves separation, loss, unanswered questions, and the lifelong search for self.

Every adoption carries a responsibility to help children understand their story, not simply how they joined their adoptive family, but what happened before. Children do not enter adoption with a blank slate. A child's need to talk about adoption helps them make meaning of their experiences, build self-esteem, develop trust, and understand their identity.

When children are not given explanations, they create their own. I know this personally. I entered foster care at 15 months old and was adopted at seven and a half. I will never forget my adoption day. My foster-adoptive family drove me to the courthouse, and I refused to get out of the car. I wrapped my arms around the seat and held on for dear life, terrified that I was being given away again because no one had explained what was happening to me.

To the adults, adoption was a legal process for permanency. To me, it felt like another separation, another terrifying moment when adults were making decisions about my life without telling me why. This is why explanations matter.

Why Children Need to Know Their Story

Children need language to make meaning. Just because a child is not asking questions does not mean they are not thinking about them. Children will wonder: Why was I adopted? Why couldn't my birth parents keep me? What were they like? Did they love me? Are you going to give me away, too?

When these questions remain unanswered, children internalize the experience as rejection. They may conclude, I must have been a bad baby, or There must be something wrong with me. Young children are egocentric. They believe they are responsible for events happening around them. And they will equate that separation from their birth family means they were unwanted or unlovable. So, they need to hear repeatedly that the separation was never their fault. They did not cause it, could not have prevented it, and were never responsible for the adults' circumstances. As I often remind children, babies are simply not that powerful.

When Should Parents Begin Telling the Story?

As early as possible. As soon as parents are educated, emotionally prepared, and have gained as much knowledge about their child’s history.

Adoption should never be presented as one dramatic disclosure. It is an ongoing conversation that must be revisited throughout childhood, a term called “recycling information.” At every new developmental stage, children will revisit facts with greater cognitive, emotional, and psychological understanding. Adoption is understood differently at age 4, 8, 12, and 16. New questions emerge as awareness develops, and information that seemed factual suddenly carries deeper emotions.

article continues after advertisement

Parents should gather photographs, letters, birth information, and gifts the birth parent may have shared. Make copies of precious photographs so children can safely hold, explore, and revisit them.

Parents should become comfortable initiating conversations rather than waiting for their child to ask, gently following the child's lead, respecting their readiness, and answering only the questions they are asking, age-appropriately.

What to Say at Different Ages

  • Ages 3–5: Keep it short and sweet. Preschool children think concretely and benefit from simple explanations, books, dolls, and pictures. Parents might explain: “You grew inside your birth mother's womb. When you were born, there were grown-up problems that made it difficult for her to care for a baby. A plan was made for another family to raise you.”
  • Ages 6–8: Help them understand why. Children begin comparing themselves with others and ask more questions about their birth family. Parents can explain: “Your birth family was experiencing difficult circumstances that made it hard to provide the care you needed. You did nothing to cause those problems. They were grown-up problems, not yours.”
  • Ages 9–12: Address shame and rejection. Children become increasingly aware of loss and may blame themselves. Reassure them: “There was nothing you did or said that caused your separation. You have always been worthy of love and care. What happened to you does not define who you are.”
  • Teenagers: Honor their need for truth and control. Adolescents need fuller explanations of their story and the circumstances surrounding their separation. Before discussing painful information about addiction, mental illness, homelessness, abuse, or neglect and learning how those circumstances affected their first family, help them understand these experiences in a broader human context.

Ask permission before sharing sensitive details. "Are you ready to learn the answer to your question?" via The Question Box Intervention from my book The Traumatized & At-Risk Youth Toolbox. A child who receives difficult information may respond with anger, disbelief, sadness, or confusion. Try not to correct these reactions; acknowledge and validate how difficult this may be to hear. Remind them that you are available to listen and support them. Also, make sure they have downtime to process and integrate this newfound information.

Words That Can Unintentionally Hurt

  • “Your mother gave you away.” Children are often separated because their parents were unable to provide safe care, meet basic needs, or manage difficult circumstances. Saying they were "given away" can reinforce feelings of rejection and abandonment.
  • “Your birth mother loved you very much.” Children may interpret this to mean that loving someone leads to separation. They may wonder whether their adoptive parents will also give them away because they love them.
  • “You were chosen because you are special.” Although well-intentioned, this statement can create pressure to remain special, grateful, or deserving. Instead, emphasize that families are formed in different ways, including adoption.
  • “Your birth parents were bad people.” Children may believe that if their birth parents were bad, something must also be wrong with them. Explain the circumstances truthfully without assigning shame or diminishing the child's birth connections.
article continues after advertisement

Utilize my children’s book What Is Adoption? For Kids with an accompanying animation to begin the dialogue:


Helping Children Feel Safe Enough to Ask Questions

Parents can become anxious or uncomfortable when their child expresses curiosity about their birth family. Children are highly sensitive to these emotional reactions and may stop asking questions to protect their parents from discomfort. Some children may even fear that expressing interest in their birth family could threaten their relationship with their adoptive parents or lead to another rejection.

If you notice yourself becoming defensive, anxious, or threatened by these conversations, I strongly encourage you to work with an adoption-competent therapist. Your child needs to know that their curiosity is not disloyalty and that their birth family can be discussed without threatening their place in your family.

The Greatest Gift Is Truth, Not Silence

So, during this month, I encourage parents to remember that explaining adoption is not about finding perfect words or eliminating painful feelings. It is about being present when children need answers, even when those answers are difficult, because we cannot change what happened to them, but we can change how they experience their past by being emotionally available in their healing.

item.title: What to Do When You’re Unsure About a Choice
item.description:
Decision-Making

What to Do When You’re Unsure About a Choice

We can ask better questions to gain insight when an important choice feels hard.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • When several choices appear to be reasonable, it may not matter which choice is made.
  • There is no singular "correct" path for one's life.
  • Instead of asking, "What's the can't-fail choice?" a more helpful question may be, "What meets my needs?"
Source: Fizkes/Shutterstock

Many people struggle with making important decisions. These include which college to attend, which career to undertake, whether to look for a new job, or how to find the right house.

One way to settle on a decision is to make a list of pros and cons of a particular course of action. A cost/benefit analysis can also help: What would the cost be for a particular choice vs. the potential benefit?

For instance, here is a simple example: Suppose you are deciding between buying two houses that differ in price. The less expensive house will have a lower down payment that would allow you to have some money left in your savings account, but it is not in a great neighborhood. The more expensive house will drain your savings, but it is in a great neighborhood.

If the neighborhood is very important to you (great benefit), it might be worthwhile to drain your savings (cost). In other words, the benefit outweighs the cost. If the neighborhood is not that important to you, then the benefit of the more expensive house would not outweigh the cost, and therefore you should buy the cheaper house.

Strategies for When There Is No Clear Choice

Sometimes, it’s hard to assess potential benefit vs. cost. For instance, if you are considering which college you want to attend, and different colleges provide different educational and extracurricular benefits that are hard to quantify, how do you make a decision?

When several colleges appear to be reasonable choices, I have a secret to share: It doesn’t matter which college you choose.

Why?

Among colleges that are a reasonable fit, what you do there matters more than which one you pick. As long as you work hard and take advantage of the educational and personal opportunities available to you at a college, you will gain a lot. If you don’t work hard and keep to yourself, you will gain little, no matter what college you attend.

Further, even if it were possible to make a “perfect” choice when you face a decision, within a few months the choice will no longer be perfect.

Why?

Because circumstances will have changed in a way that affects the benefits and potential costs of your decision.

For instance, if the decision you made related to choosing an undergraduate school, your preferences will likely change once you are exposed to new ideas, people, and situations that may alter your college experience in unforeseeable ways.

Bottom line: Even with important decisions, pick one, and make the best of it. In most circumstances, you will do well. If that does not turn out to be the case, you often can change course, and will have become wiser because you will be able to figure out how to avoid making a similar wrong choice in the future.

Another secret to keep in mind is: There is no "one" correct path for your life. People don’t click along straight lines like trains on railroad tracks. We float and bob and turn like rafts on a river that’s always flowing and changing.

You may feel like you can’t afford to make any “wrong” decisions—but sometimes the less obvious choice is a great one that will create new possibilities for you.

On my Center Point podcast, I have interviewed many successful people. I’ve been struck by many of the interviewees who changed course a few times until they identified their main career when they were in their late 20s.

Further, keep in mind that many people change jobs often, especially early in their working lives (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so your first choice is unlikely to lock you in permanently. With these secrets in mind, let’s look at thinking patterns that can help make good choices:

1. Ask the right question.

Instead of asking, "What's the can't-fail choice?" consider asking, "What meets my needs?" Instead of "What could go wrong?" ask, "What are the possibilities? Instead of "What will everyone else think?" ask, "What is right for me?" When you ask these questions, you give your inner wisdom a chance to help guide you.

2. Be flexible and hopeful.

Some of the greatest blessings that come into our lives are surprises. When a decision doesn’t play out the way you want or expect, think about how you can embrace your new direction or challenge instead of ways you can be unhappy about it. For instance, when you decide to audition for a part in the school play and don’t get chosen, think of what you can do with all the free time you’ll have.

3. Time travel.

When you feel stuck about a decision, imagine how your future self will feel about your choice—maybe in a month, a year, or even 10 years. What advice would the future wiser, older version of you give? Let the answer help guide your choices today.

4. Be like Batman (or Sasha Fierce!).

Did you know that there’s a scientific principle called the Batman Effect? It’s just as cool as it sounds. Also known as self-distancing, this is the idea that you can create a little space, perspective, and extra strength to deal with any decision or situation by getting out of an “I” mindset. In one study, researchers asked people to give a small public speech. (Speaking in public is a common and severe fear.)

One group was asked to think about the upcoming speech as if they were in the middle of it, making statements that started with “I am” and “I feel.” Another group was asked to consider the same things, but instead of using an “I feel” statement, a participant named Anne would say, “Anne feels” or “Anne thinks.”

It seems like a small change, right? But the results weren’t small. Participants who used the third person were less afraid and anxious, and they gave better speeches (Streamer et al,. 2017).

In a study with young children, researchers found they could take this idea one step further by having kids consider what Batman would do. Kids who were thinking like Batman were found to have thought more clearly than all the other participants (White & Carlson, 2015).

This kind of thinking is not just for kids. Years ago, when Beyoncé was explaining how she gives commanding live performances, she explained that when she was ready to go on stage, she’d stop thinking of herself as a regular person and start thinking of herself as a strong, powerful performer called Sasha Fierce. Sasha Fierce was confident and bold, and she helped make Beyoncé one of the top-selling recording artists of all time.

Takeaway

Making important decisions can be stressful, especially when we worry that one wrong choice could change the course of our lives. But there is rarely just one correct path. By considering our options thoughtfully, asking ourselves helpful questions, and remaining flexible about what comes next, we can approach decisions with greater confidence.

Parts of this post are excerpted from my book, The Life Guide for Teens.

item.title: Living Long Enough for the Next New Treatment
item.description:
Anxiety

Living Long Enough for the Next New Treatment

Personal Perspective: Connecting with others to ease the anxiety.

Posted November 16, 2026

My wife, Christine, had to fly out to London for work after missing several trips due to my illness. Before she left, I had gotten my follow-up CT scan, but the radiologist hadn't read it yet. I had significant “scanxiety” about what it would show. While Christine was away, my kids did their best to help me—waking up on their own (tough as teens), fixing their own breakfast (really tough as teens), and getting out the door (really, really tough as teens). They even loaded and unloaded the dishwasher! Even though we had most of the logistics covered sans Mommy, the house was twice as dirty as usual. Plus, I missed the emotional anchor of her presence. The house was quieter. The click-clack of her keyboard or murmur of her work video calls was absent.

I received the CT report a couple of days into Christine’s trip. Good news! The cancer in my right lung and a spot in my liver had shrunk. Being anxious, I got the report right away from my friend and primary care provider. That night, when I was showering, I was gripped with a sudden, unexpected sadness that verged on depression. Despite the positive results, in the back of my mind, I’d had this deep hope that my cancer would have magically vanished. Instead, the cancer, though smaller, was still there. The study my treatment was based on had shown that one patient had been miraculously noted in complete remission. It was just one point on a chart in a study, but the hope that it would happen for me had gripped my mind. I went into a negative-feedback cycle, and I was choked up, on the verge of tears. Somehow I had turned my good news into something horrible. Usually, I’d talk about the results and my hopes and fears, but she was a continent away and fast asleep. I made it through the week and to the eighth class, but the experience was a poignant reminder of how important this was to my mental well-being; sharing my experiences with others still is.

Early on in my diagnosis, I called my classmate and good friend from medical school, who practices pulmonology in San Diego. I wasn’t close to any other classmates in med school except for Elan—we bonded over Mike’s Roast Beef sandwiches while taking our physical diagnosis class. He kindly reviewed my tests and introduced me to another friend and colleague, who told me something that gives me hope every day: “You only have to live long enough for the next new treatment to come out.” That simple statement comforts me when I dwell on my late-stage prognosis, thinking about how many years (or months) I may have left.

One of the many beautiful parts of sharing my own cancer journey is meeting people going through their own cancer journeys who I would never have met otherwise. Sharing personal narratives—whether through storytelling, group discussions, or expressive writing—has emerged as a valuable psychosocial intervention in oncology. Storytelling is the communicative act of patients recounting their illness experiences through words, images, or even digital media, often revealing deeply personal emotions and insights. Across cancer types and patient populations, narrative-sharing interventions are increasingly recognized for fostering emotional expression and psychological adaptation to illness. Peer-reviewed research spanning children, adolescents, adults, and the elderly, indicates that storytelling bestows a range of benefits. These benefits include improvements in psychological well-being, coping and resilience, treatment adherence, social support, and even physiological or clinical outcomes.

Peer-reviewed research overwhelmingly supports the therapeutic value of storytelling and personal narratives for cancer patients of all ages and stages. Through sharing their experiences—whether in a support group, with a counselor, via digital media, or in a private journal—patients often achieve better psychological well-being, characterized by reduced anxiety, stress, and even depression. Storytelling fosters adaptation and coping, empowering patients with resilience and practical strategies to face cancer’s challenges. It also enhances social connectedness, diminishing isolation and strengthening support networks among those who “get it.” Notably, narrative interventions can encourage patients to stay engaged in treatment and healthy behaviors, potentially improving adherence and follow-through in care. While more research is needed, emerging evidence points to physiological benefits—improved symptom control, functional status, and overall quality of life—arising from the mind-body interplay of expressive storytelling. Taken together, these studies support the belief that the simple act of sharing one’s story is far more than talk or writing on a page; it is a meaningful therapeutic process that can help cancer patients heal psychologically, cope more effectively, build community, and perhaps even influence their health trajectories for the better. Narrative practices in oncology—from diagnosis through survivorship or end-of-life care—represent a holistic approach that honors patients’ voices while delivering measurable benefits across multiple dimensions of well-being.

Scans, treatments, family, and faith shape mental health; this can get wrapped into the stories people tell themselves when the future becomes a moving target. Narrative medicine is not a soft add-on to “real” care; it is part of the human need to communicate and be heard.

item.title: What Do We Do With Leftover Love?
item.description:
Infidelity

What Do We Do With Leftover Love?

Lingering love after betrayal is not a sign that you are weak.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Discovering betrayal takes seconds, but the brain needs longer to loosen attachment.
  • Lingering love can be used to pressure a person into abandoning their values and judgment.
  • Deception is psychological abuse and a tool of coercive control.

He was everything you had ever wanted. Kind, gentle, thoughtful. Almost too good to be true. You imagined a future together, a home, a family, a lifetime of ordinary mornings. Then, one day, while making eggs for breakfast, you saw the messages. The pan was still warm. The sun was coming through the window. Nothing around you had changed, yet it's all gone. In a matter of seconds, the man you thought you knew disappeared. The future you had imagined vanished with him. But the love you felt still lingers.

You can throw the eggs into the bin, but the feelings cannot disappear as quickly. Love involves several interconnected brain systems. Dopamine-rich reward pathways contribute to desire and anticipation (Fisher et al., 2010); the brain's natural opioid system helps make closeness comforting and social rejection distressing (Hsu et al., 2013; Nummenmaa et al., 2016); and limbic regions, particularly the amygdala, help connect emotional experiences with memory (Cahill et al., 1996). The truth can change what you think in seconds, but it cannot instantly erase what your brain has learned over months or years, so do not let people tell you that you are "co-dependent" or "weak." You have a normal brain that might play tricks on you.

The Cruelty of Weaponized Love

You have leftover love, and that leftover love can be weaponised against you (Lesiak & Gelsthorpe, 2025). He may use the feelings that remain to persuade you to let him stay, asking you to ignore what you have discovered, silence your judgment, and compromise the very values that define who you are.

He has already betrayed you. Now he is asking you to betray yourself for him.

You are the one expected to swallow your anger, silence your judgment, and call it "forgiveness." Look at the bargain. He gets to keep the woman who loves him. And you are expected to give up the woman who knows the truth.

Decades ago, psychiatrist Judith Herman wrote about it in Trauma and Recovery (1992):

His ultimate goal appears to be the creation of a willing victim. Hostages, political prisoners, battered women, and slaves have all remarked upon the captor’s curious psychological dependence upon his victim. George Orwell gives voice to the totalitarian mind in the novel 1984:

“We are not content with negative obedience, nor even with the most abject submission. When finally you surrender to us, it must be of your own free will. We do not destroy the heretic because he resists us; so long as he resists us we never destroy him. We convert him, we capture his inner mind, we reshape him. We burn all evil and all illusion out of him; we bring him over to our side, not in appearance, but genuinely, heart and soul.”

Read those last words again. Heart and soul.

It is not enough that you stay. You must want to stay. It is not enough that you forgive him. You must learn to see his betrayal as something you can live with. You must look at the evidence of your own eyes and persuade yourself that it no longer matters.

And if keeping him means abandoning everything you believe in, what exactly are you trying to save—and what's left—when you do that?

Some wounds are easier to bear because you know you stood by your values while receiving them. In Kraków, officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański were seriously wounded confronting a mass shooter. Poland calls them heroes, and people across the country are grateful for their courage and service.

Then there is another kind of wound. One that no surgeon can stitch. Amy Winehouse sings it in "You Know I'm No Good": “I cheated myself, like I knew I would.” By the end of the song, she is no longer simply confessing what she did. She is passing judgment on herself.

Imagine waking up beside a man you no longer respect, living a life you never wanted, having persuaded yourself to accept things you once knew were unacceptable. You kept him, perhaps. But somewhere along the way, you lost the ability to trust your own judgment.

That is the deeper cruelty of weaponised love (Lesiak & Gelsthorpe, 2025). He does not need you to believe he is innocent. He needs you to stop caring that he isn't.

And if manipulation or coercion brought you to that point, the shame belongs to the person who engineered that surrender, not to you.

What to Do About Leftover Love

  1. Rewrite the story, this time with the truth. Look back with what you now know. His unexplained moods. The jokes that weren't really jokes. When he laughed that he was seeing "lots of people", perhaps he was telling the truth. Those sweet early goodnight texts? He was on his way to another woman's house. Stop protecting the beautiful story he sold you.
  2. Talk, talk, talk. And write. Tell your story to people you trust. Write down what happened, what you discovered, and how it changed your understanding of the relationship. Betrayal creates confusion, and nostalgia has a remarkable talent for editing out the ugly parts. When you start missing him, return to the facts. Don't let loneliness become his defence lawyer.

  3. Name the man, not the fantasy. The betrayal wasn't simply another woman. It was the months of lies that made you believe you were building a future together while he was living another life. He needed you to trust him because, had you known the truth, you might have walked away. So he made sure you didn't.

    That is what a programme of deception does. It robs you of the freedom to make informed choices about your own life. When used to dominate and subordinate, deception becomes a tool of coercive control and psychological abuse. Stop reaching for words that make him sound better. A liar is a liar. A traitor is a traitor. A backstabber is a backstabber. Grieve the man he pretended to be, the image he created to win your love and use it to control you. But don't defend the man behind the mask.

  4. Take back your loyalty. You were loyal to a man who betrayed you. That loyalty was something beautiful about you, but in the wrong hands it became a weapon. You do not owe him your silence, your protection, your forgiveness, or another chance. Stop making decisions around his comfort. Go where you want to go. Do what you want to do. Build the life you want. Be loyal to yourself.

The eggs went into the bin that morning. The relationship ended. The feelings are disappearing. You'll be ok! Probably you are already more ok now than when you were cheated on, lied to, and abused.

item.title: HIV Treatment Is Prevention
item.description:
Health

HIV Treatment Is Prevention

The message of HIV treatment as prevention resonates with some more than others.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • When people living with HIV have an undetectable viral load, they cannot transmit the virus through sex.
  • Sexual minority men in non-monogamous relationships with uninfected partners had the best HIV outcomes.
  • Prevention messaging may be less relevant for those in relationships where both partners are living with HIV.

HIV treatment, antiretroviral therapy (ART), has seen dramatic advancement in the past four decades. HIV is now a chronic condition. When people take their ART as prescribed and maintain an undetectable viral load and a high T-cell count, life expectancy for those living with HIV approximates that of those who are uninfected (Trickey et al., 2023).

In addition to the direct health benefits of maintaining an undetectable viral load, there is an additional prevention benefit. When someone living with HIV has an undetectable viral load, they are unable to transmit HIV through sex (Eisinger et al., 2019). Public health campaigns promoting ART adherence have called attention to this phenomenon, terming it Undetectable = Untransmissible or U=U.

How Relationship Status May Influence Motivation to Adhere to HIV Treatment

We might assume that prevention messaging that draws on U=U would be most effective among people living with HIV who are partnered with someone who is uninfected. Having an undetectable viral load would decrease or eliminate the potential for sexual transmission of HIV to their partner. Alternatively, people living with HIV may be generally motivated to take their ART and maintain an undetectable viral load when they are having sex with partners who may be uninfected regardless of relationship status.

In two recent studies (Hillesheim & Starks, 2026; Starks et al., 2024), our team examined relationship status group differences in ART adherence and viral detectability in large samples of sexual minority male adults.

Ordinarily, we expect people in relationships to have better health outcomes compared to single people (Kiecolt-Glaser & Wilson, 2017). In both of these papers, findings suggested this was true for sexual minority men living with HIV in non-monogamous relationships and those whose partners were uninfected. These groups were more likely to be adherent to ART and report an undetectable viral load compared to single sexual minority men. Presumably, these are groups where men may be most likely to consider preventing transmission of HIV to sexual partners.

There was also a warning sign in both papers. Sexual minority men in relationships where both partners were living with HIV were significantly less likely to be adherent to their ART and achieve an undetectable viral load. For these men, prevention motivation may be of limited relevance. It may be important to emphasize the personal health benefits of HIV treatment to maximize HIV outcomes in these subgroups.

Tailoring HIV Treatment Messages to Personal Health Benefits

Effective HIV treatment not only prolongs the lives of people living with HIV, but it also eliminates the potential for sexual transmission. This prevention motivation may explain why rates of ART adherence and achieving an undetectable viral load are higher among sexual minority men in non-monogamous relationships and those with uninfected partners. We may need different messages, emphasizing the personal health benefits of HIV care, to reach subgroups who have low levels of sexual HIV prevention motivation.

item.title: What Might We Lose When Death Is Kept at a Distance?
item.description:
Relationships

What Might We Lose When Death Is Kept at a Distance?

My father died in hospital. Home death care made me rethink goodbye.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Some families choose to care for a loved one’s body at home after death.
  • Home death care can involve practical tasks as well as time with the deceased.
  • How quickly the body leaves may shape how families experience death and goodbye.

Death is everywhere, yet for much of my life I have encountered it only in glimpses. As a scholar with the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath, I regularly encounter different perspectives on death and dying. My own experiences, though, have felt brief and distant.

In my 20s, I visited my grandma in hospital. She had suffered a stroke that would prove fatal. I remember gasping quietly as I entered the room. Something about her contorted face, laboured breathing, and pained expression shocked me.

I felt relieved when I was told visiting hours were over. I left the ward feeling sick to my stomach.

At funerals over the years, I watched a succession of coffins disappear behind plush curtains: Grandma, Grandpa, Nana, Uncle Chris, Aunty Lil, Aunty Rachael, Aunty Mary, and Uncle Mick.

Looking back, these were glimpses of death and dying: processes that felt detached, as though they somehow existed outside my life.

Dad Dying

It was much the same with Dad. I got the call from a hospital consultant around 11 p.m.

“I’m sorry, but your dad is now unconscious,” he told me.

“I’d suggest coming to visit him as soon as you can. There’s nothing more we can do but keep him comfortable.”

This was it. Dad was dying. I drove through the night.

The curtain was drawn around his bed when the nurse guided me to his cubicle. I was terrified of what I’d see. Again, I wanted to run away when I first saw him lying there, occasionally flinching, his face slightly contorted, struggling for breath, no longer fully alive.

I asked for a little time alone with him, and the nurse told me she thought he could still hear me. “Leslie! Leslie…” she said loudly, gently shaking his shoulder as though she was trying to wake him from a deep sleep. “There's someone here to see you, Leslie. That's nice, isn't it?”

I had things I wanted to tell Dad. I wanted him to know that I loved him, and that wherever he was going next, I hoped he would find peace.

I also felt a need to touch him. At first, I touched his arm, like a child prodding something mysterious they have found in a rock pool. As my reticence evaporated, I placed the palm of my hand gently on his skin, closed my eyes, and spoke.

“I love you, Dad. And Em, and Mum, and Joe—they told me to tell you they love you too.”

He died five days later. At his funeral, I watched his coffin disappear behind a pair of curtains.

Caring for the Dead at Home

Recently, I examined an excellent Ph.D. thesis on home death care in the United Kingdom. It explored the experiences of a small group of people who chose to care for a loved one’s body at home before the funeral.

For various personal reasons, they chose to care for a loved one’s body at home after death—sometimes after the person had died elsewhere. They became, in the words used in the research, “custodians of the dead.”

I read their stories with interest.

The practical commitment could be considerable. Depending on the circumstances, caring for the body could involve washing or dressing it, repositioning it, preparing a room, and deciding who could visit. If the body remained at home for several days, arrangements also had to be made to keep it cool. Families described living alongside a body that cooled, stiffened, and gradually changed.

The experience also gave people time and space to confront things they might otherwise not have been able to. They began to make sense of a loved one’s transition from living person to dead body, taking a closer look at death itself.

Keeping the deceased at home for an extended period also allowed people to say goodbye at a slower, more organic pace. One woman described talking to her mother as she cleaned the living room, commenting on the birds, the sky, and the trees, just as she had when her mother was alive.

Home death care will not suit every person or family. The thesis focused on people who chose it, and we also need to hear from those who found the experience difficult or regretted it.

What Might We Lose When We Hold Death at a Distance?

As I listened, I thought about Dad and the short time I spent with him as he lay dying in hospital. My experience sits within a broader shift.

The Lancet Commission on the Value of Death describes how, over generations, dying has moved from family and community settings toward health systems, where it is often treated primarily as a medical or physiological event. In England in 2023, hospital was the most common place of death: 42.8 percent of people died there. Another 28.4 percent died at home and 21 percent in care homes.

The separation can continue after death. Research on home death care in England describes how the body is commonly moved to a mortuary or funeral home, where its care passes to professionals. I began to wonder what this separation from the body might mean for the people closest to someone who has died.

What might it have been like if I’d had the chance to be with Dad in the way the people in the thesis had been with their loved ones? Might I have moved through my initial shock and experienced something beyond it? Would our goodbye have felt different? And might I have begun to relate to death and dying in a way I can’t quite fathom now, when the physical experience of death feels so far removed from my life?

item.title: The Spice Rack Brain Hack
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

The Spice Rack Brain Hack

Adding a little spice to your food can kick up your gut-brain axis.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Spices contain polyphenols, plant chemicals that act as antioxidants and reduce inflammation.
  • Polyphenols support healthy microbes.
  • Healthy microbes produce substances that can improve mood, cognition, and memory.
Source: Midjourney

“He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert

Spice adds variety to your life. Especially in your microbiome. Studies are increasingly finding that spices can boost the variety of good microbes in your gut. That, in turn, can improve your mood and cognition via the gut-brain axis.

A study by Regina Lamendella and colleagues, published in The Journal of Nutrition, found that blends of herbs and spices—including cinnamon, ginger, cumin, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, basil, and thyme—increased diversity of the microbiome, a measure of health. The best results were with the participants who got the largest dose of spices—about 1 ½ teaspoons a day.

Polyphenols in Spices Fight Inflammation and Feed the Gut

What is so great about spices and herbs? Their main attraction is their high levels of polyphenols—plant chemicals that provide flavor and color. People who eat plenty of polyphenol-rich foods can cut their risk of type 2 diabetes in half and improve their heart health.

Polyphenols suppress enzymes that activate inflammation. They are also antioxidants, further helping to quell inflammation. Cloves have about 15 percent polyphenols by weight, whereas veggies may have only 0.1 percent. Along with their intrinsic anti-inflammatory effects, polyphenols act as prebiotic fiber, feeding your beneficial gut microbes.

How Butyrate and the Gut-Brain Axis Connect Spices to Brain Health

The researchers saw an increase in microbes that produce butyrate, an amazing substance that nourishes and heals the cells lining your gut, ensuring that they keep toxins and pathogens out of your bloodstream. Butyrate does more: It can travel to the brain, encouraging the growth of new nerve cells, improving cognition and memory.

The gut-brain axis responds to inflammation by putting you into sickness mode, where you just want to be left alone to lie in bed while your joy evaporates. This behavior is pretty much identical to depression. Depression and anxiety overlap strongly with gut issues, and psychiatrists are increasingly turning to prebiotics and probiotics to augment other treatments. Microbes that can improve your mood are called psychobiotics. While polyphenols boost good bacteria, they also fight harmful bacteria like C. difficile, Salmonella, and E. coli.

Historical Uses of Spices

It's not exactly news that spices are healthy. Some 2,500 years ago, Hippocrates believed that spices like cinnamon, coriander, and saffron had healing powers. Nutmeg was prescribed for flatulence, and enticingly, ginger was used as an aphrodisiac. The Kama Sutra recommends cardamom, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves for a good time. Spices were, and still are, sexy.

Spices were also expensive. In 410 AD, the Visigoths sacked Rome and held it hostage for a ransom of 5,000 pounds of gold and 3,000 pounds of pepper. At the time, spices were as good as gold. In those days, traders conspired to restrict the supply of spices, ensuring high prices. Their trade routes were kept secret, and excess crops were burned. It was a cutthroat business, but smuggled seeds soon cropped up in tropical farms around the world. Today, supply chains are efficient, and spices are far cheaper, so there’s little to stop you from trying some.

Easy Ways to Add Spices to Everyday Meals

I live in Ohio, where salt and pepper are the top spices. Mexican and Thai foods have been tamed for the timid tongues of my townies. But you don’t have to succumb to the blandness of the Midwest. You can kick it up a notch. Add some cinnamon to your oatmeal. Try cardamom or star anise in cookies or add whole pods when cooking rice or lentils (don’t forget to fish them out before serving. In my house, anyone who complains about a leftover spice pod gets to do the dishes).

Don't be afraid to play with combinations of spices to create your own custom spice blend. Use it as a rub on fish or meat before cooking or sprinkle some spice on food after it’s cooked. Pro tip: Buy spices whole and grind them just before using to get the maximum joy. Spices have a lot of volatile oils that evaporate over time and deplete the magnificent aromas.

Start Slowly With Spices if Necessary

If you have GERD or IBS, start slowly. Spices activate microbes, which can create gas if you overdo it. But over time, your microbes will adjust.

For everyone else, spices are awesome. They may not help you control the universe, but they taste great, and they can improve your mood. Once you get started, you’ll realize that life is too short to be stuck with bland food. Kick it up a notch.

item.title: Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?
item.description:
Loneliness

Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

Easing loneliness is not the same as building human connection.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Despite its positives, AI poses potential threats to meaning, character, and especially human relationships.
  • Easing loneliness with AI may weaken the drive to seek deeper human connection.
  • AI companionship risks harming communities, not just individual users.

Engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier. Undoubtedly, some uses will prove beneficial, and others harmful. Evaluating the effect of different forms of AI engagement on human flourishing will thus be critical, and we believe our flourishing measure provides a helpful framework by which to do so. The effects of AI on flourishing may also differ across domains of flourishing.

The Potential for AI and Flourishing

There may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security. It is not guaranteed to do so, and indeed, as per Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity), much of what AI does or does not achieve will depend upon whether the human person and human dignity are made central in the use and diffusion of AI. However, if employed well and equitably, the potential for AI to advance these aspects of human well-being may be substantial.

The effects, however, of AI technologies on more humanistic aspects of well-being, such as meaning, character, or relationships, seem more ambiguous. Rich, developed countries already seem to be struggling with these more humanistic aspects of well-being, possibly in part due to technology. Will AI help or hinder our sense of meaning, our character, our relationships? As always, so much depends on how we use it.

AI and Relationships

AI technologies with various relational elements have effectively been used for purposes ranging from helping autistic children develop social skills to building the capacity of university students for civil discourse. While such uses arguably always ought to point back to real relationships, these systems may indeed have the potential to truly enhance human relationships.

However, there is another class of chatbots that aims not at enhancing human relationships, but at replacing them. These are chatbots whose principal aim and purpose is friendship and romance. In a recent article, we have argued that such friendship and romance chatbots have no place in a flourishing life. This may seem like an extreme position. After all, what harm is there in having loneliness somewhat relieved if one’s friends or family are proving disappointing?

The problem is that the temporary alleviation of loneliness is not a solution to loneliness. Loneliness, as painful as it can be, is experienced precisely to try to direct our attention, and our longings, towards deeper human connection. That can take a lot of work and time, and may not be fully within our grasp. But that thirst for human connection has a fundamental role in our life, in guiding us towards others.

When AI chatbots have, as their goal, not helping us with human relationships, but replacing them, they will do damage—damage to ourselves, damage to those we might have interacted with, and damage to the social fabric of society. If they satisfy our loneliness, they do so without another person. A chatbot that always seems to understand, that never has needs of its own, that treats neglect with a delight to see us, ultimately makes us weaker in our capacity for real human relationships. We come to have unrealistic expectations of what to hope for in real human relationships. We lose the capacity to grow through the very difficulties and frictions that real human relationships entail. We come to focus on ourselves rather than on providing for the needs of others. Indeed, with AI friendship and romance, there is no one on the other side to whose life we have contributed.

Society and AI Relationships

While AI may have some capacity to enhance our relationships (pointing us towards helpful books or resources for particular problems we are wrestling with) and while certain AI chatbot applications may benefit from relational elements (like the training programs above), this is very different from AI chatbots aimed at replacing real relationships. The effects of these are universally and comprehensively detrimental. They harm us, and they harm those around us. Even if we do not feel the negative effects now, or if they seem small, the increasing incapacity for social relationships will over time gradually erode human connection, human community, and the fabric of society. Human relationships are critical for our health and well-being.

In a remarkable turn of events, China, which has been very pro-AI, in July put into place comprehensive legislation restricting the development and marketing of AI tools “that provide emotional care, companionship, support, and other emotional services,” and including a strict ban on tools “excessively pandering to users, inducing emotional reliance or addiction, [or] harming users' relationships with real people.” What does China know that we don’t? They seem to have almost presciently anticipated the likely effects of AI romance and relationships on human society, human relationships, human reproduction, and human community.

There have also recently been some helpful legislative efforts here in the United States, especially for minors. However, we are naïve to think children are the only ones at risk.

While we do think a ban on AI “relationship chatbots” for friendship and romance may be reasonable here (after all, we ban heroin in the United States), some might view such measures as too extreme. Even if so, we nevertheless believe every effort should be made in practice to purge AI friendship and romance from our lives as individuals and as communities. A technology designed to replace human connection is not a neutral technology.

Building a Civilization of Love

Love—including love of neighbor and even love of enemy—is crucial for the flourishing of our society. In the words of Pope Leo (and others before him), if we are to seek a flourishing society (and to do so in the age of AI), we need to build “a civilization of love.” We need to love and care for one another. We need to be with one another. We need to have the capacity to work through the difficulties and frictions that real relationships entail, and to grow through those struggles. Therein lies our flourishing, for ourselves, for others, and for society. Real human love requires real human people.

item.title: Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers
item.description:
Autism

Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers

Eye-tracking, barrier tests, and spontaneous messages tell a different story.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Nonspeaking spellers looked at letters before pointing and hit 94% accuracy, a pattern cueing can’t explain.
  • With no one holding the device, nonspeaking autistic people still showed they knew how to spell.
  • Spellers express wishes their families never expected, the kind of authorship evidence cueing can’t produce.
  • Blocking spellers’ view of their partner, the equivalent of Hans’s blinders, didn’t stop them from spelling.

Every time nonspeaking people with autism who spell to communicate make the news, someone brings up Clever Hans. You may know the story: In early 1900s Berlin, a horse seemed to do math, tapping out answers with his hoof. In 1907, the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed what was really going on. When the questioner knew the answer and Hans could see them, Hans was right about 89% of the time; when the questioner didn't know, or Hans wore blinders, he dropped to about 6%. Questioners unknowingly leaned forward while he tapped and relaxed when he reached the right number, and Hans had learned to stop there.

The suggestion is that spellers are doing the same thing: that the words really come from the person holding the letterboard, either through subtle cues or through the communication partner's unconscious movements (the ideomotor effect). In this post, I draw on my own data and on a year of observations of nonspeaking autistic people to show why this analogy doesn't hold, and why it should be dropped for good. This is not only my personal opinion that comparing nonspeaking autistic people to a horse is cruel; it is also what the facts show.

Why spelling isn't counting

Hans's trick worked because his task was simple: all he needed was a signal telling him when to stop tapping. Spelling is a different kind of task. To spell a sentence, a person has to choose the right letter out of 26, in the right order, again and again. A single "stop" cue, the kind that worked for Hans, can't do that. Add to this complex dance the sentences that contain words the communication partner doesn't know or normally use, or information nobody in the room expected to hear.

The best evidence here comes from studies that measured how spellers actually spell. In 2020, Vikram Jaswal and his colleagues fitted nine nonspeaking autistic letterboard users with head-mounted eye-trackers while they answered questions about an article read aloud to them, with an assistant holding the board.¹ They pointed to about one letter per second, and 94% of the letters they pointed to were correct. On average, they looked at 71% of the correct letters before pointing to them, about half a second ahead. Like fluent non-autistic typists, they paused longer before the first letter of a new word and were faster on common letter pairs. As the authors point out, cueing would require a separate signal for every letter, picked from 26 options, which would be slow and error-prone. What they found was fast, accurate, and planned.

Some critics argue that the partner moves the board slightly toward the right letter. A 2024 study from the same lab removed the partner entirely.² Thirty-one nonspeaking autistic teenagers and adults played a game on an iPad mounted on a stand, tapping letters as they lit up. No one held the iPad. As a group, they tapped faster when the letters spelled a sentence they had just heard than when similar letters or symbols came in a meaningless order. They were also faster on common letter pairs, and they paused before the first letter of each new word. These are signs of knowing how to spell.

A third study had participants spell on a virtual letterboard in an augmented-reality headset, with no one holding it; they averaged 95.8% accuracy on dictated words.³

If spellers were reading their partners the way Hans read his questioners, blocking their view of the partner should stop them, just as the blinders stopped Hans. As it happens, we've been testing this with a few spellers by placing a rigid panel, about five feet tall and three feet wide, between the speller and the communication partner, so that the spellers cannot see the partners' faces or bodies. The results? They keep spelling fluently and without hesitation. After the very first word, one of them even spelled: "Better with the barrier."

Messages nobody knew or expected

The second problem with the horse analogy is the content. Hans only ever answered questions, and only with answers the questioner already had in mind. Spellers start conversations, ask for things, and say things that surprise the people around them.

A young man I visited this year began spelling at fifteen and spells mainly with his mother. After I spent a full day visiting him at school, he was able that evening to have a conversation about his day and to spell the names of two kids who had visited the classroom; neither his mother nor I knew their names, and his mother hadn't been at school. He was also able to express his feelings towards his brothers and his wish for more independence: "I'm seventeen, let me go by myself," he spelled when he asked to walk to the bus stop alone. Among his other wishes, he asked to go into the ocean with his brothers, wearing a life jacket, and told his parents he wanted a North Face backpack, not the Under Armour one they had picked.

When his mother first began spelling with him on her own, one of his first requests was to see a Broadway show, which she had never imagined he wanted. He also spelled things his partner would not choose to hear. In front of me, he told his mother that a book I'd brought was boring, and she was embarrassed. On another occasion, when he came downstairs while his mother was out, he spelled to his father: "Dad, stop giving me chicken nuggets. I just want to spend time together."

But perhaps his most unexpected request came when he spelled out that he wanted to go to Disney World for his sixteenth birthday, something the family would never have expected, given his sensitivity to crowded and noisy places. They went; he wore noise-cancelling headphones, and he had a blast. "I tolerated it because I wanted to be there," he told me, and made fun of how his father threw up on rides.

A cueing account says the words come from his mother's expectations. However, these messages went against what his family expected, and they changed how the family lives with him. This is exactly what we should be looking for when we ask whether a speller is the author of their words: requests, opinions, and jokes that the partner did not anticipate and would not have chosen. The Hans model has no way to produce them.

Why this matters

Comparing a person to a horse responding to signals is not a neutral choice. It fits an old and outdated assumption: that people who don't speak don't understand. For decades, nonspeaking autistic people were labeled profoundly intellectually disabled, often without any assessment that accommodated their motor differences. The young man I visited spent his early school years in a program built around life skills and weather charts, and he calls his current high school classroom what it is: segregated. When a speller's words are dismissed with a one-line reference to Clever Hans, the speller pays the price: in which school they attend, whether their requests are taken seriously, and whether anyone asks for their opinion at all.

And, if you are still not convinced after reading this, perhaps hearing from the nonspeakers themselves will help. Here’s what they have been expressing about the effects of spelling on their lives:

"It was a game changer for me. It provided me with freedom I dreamed about for 15 years. Now, instead of being an observer, I am an active participant."

"Learning to spell changed my life trajectory. Before, I was treated like a toddler, and my world collapsed in on me… doctors, experts, teachers got it all wrong.… So communication is not just a basic need but a human right."

"It makes my life worth living."

Sit with them.

item.title: Making Change Happen
item.description:
Personality Change

Making Change Happen

Learn how to get out of your own way to make those needed changes.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • People struggle to change even when they genuinely want to.
  • Changing key aspects of yourself can seem insurmountable.
  • Here are five key principles that can help you make change happen.

So, you realize that the way you have been going about things doesn’t work. You might not like the way you behave or your experience of relationships. You might not like the way you feel or how your emotions impact your decisions. And you know that if you don’t turn things around, you are going to keep repeating the same cycle. But people often struggle to change even when they genuinely want to.

I cringe when I hear people say “That’s just the way I am” while at the same time complaining about the state of their relationships. Some people use that statement to avoid responsibility. They believe their personality characteristics are fixed or have repeatedly failed in their efforts to foster change within themselves. So, rather than putting effort into changing themselves, many people prefer that others would simply come to their senses and accommodate them.

You can always work on changing the environment, and this is usually what people try first. They try to convince, persuade, nudge, and manipulate others… or they shut themselves off interpersonally, go into denial, or resort to blame and attack. But these efforts rarely result in lasting positive outcomes, and people stay happy only as long as the environment is cooperating.

Here is my recommended outline for lasting change and understanding why change can be so hard. I recommend taking these steps sequentially, as they build on each other in a cumulative fashion.

1. What are you trying to change?

If you want to change yourself, you first need to consider what “self” you are referring to. Changing your entire being may seem insurmountable and lead you to give up before you even start. But many psychological theorists view the self as multifaceted. In other words, we are all groupings of associated parts, and we can use our more developed parts to help shape and coach the less developed ones that we are trying to change.

Sometimes change means de-emphasizing one previously dominant part of your personality and strengthening a part that was previously dormant.

2. Addressing your ambivalence

People are often ambivalent about change and might actually get something out of maintaining their negative behaviors.

Before you lay aside your own ambivalence, let’s see what you actually get out of the behavior or experience you say you want to let go of. What will you lose if you change? What are the factors arguing against it?

Become conscious of your own resistance. Before evoking your commitment to a new course of action, it might help to first write down all of the positive things you get out of it. For example, what if you want to cut down on your drinking? Drinking might help you gain social acceptance and feel less lonely. It might help you relax and escape your anxiety and internal demons. Or it might simply help you escape boredom and give you something to do. These are all reasonable goals, and before you lay down the booze, you might want to consider how you are going to meet them.

3. You may want to change a behavior pattern….

But then you must ask yourself, what would need to change first before the behavior can change? Problematic behaviors are often not consciously chosen but, rather, come about through how we regulate our emotions— for example, putting too much pressure on an ambivalent romantic partner, talking too much about your insecurities, or getting aggravated and shutting down when interactions with a relationship partner get touchy.

In these examples, the root cause is often difficulty controlling your emotions.

Sometimes, your rational brain knows what it wants to do, but your emotional brain just won’t cooperate.

You should learn about how people with your personality style regulate anxiety. For example, a person with an avoidant attachment style will most likely regulate anxiety by withdrawing, shutting down, or dominating. A person with an anxious attachment style is most likely to regulate emotions by pressing too hard for reassurance or oversharing.

Learn about your personality and attachment style… then you will have an easier time changing your behavior. In other words, your conscious brain will understand what your emotional brain is doing and how to keep it from taking over.

Sometimes you just need an attitude adjustment. In the preceding paragraphs, I outlined how subconscious processes, like regulating emotions, influence behavior. But sometimes, behavior comes from the more conscious parts of your mind. In other words, your emotions follow your thoughts instead of the other way around. Attitudes are consciously held statements that you tell yourself about the way things are. You can change your attitudes by watching your self-talk and what you say to yourself in your head. Don’t expect to have angry, intolerant thoughts and be able to pull off controlling your emotions and acting loving.

4. Practice emotional containment and anchor yourself

If you want to change a part of yourself, it often helps to have another part supervise the process and give you supportive feedback. Take the example of inner child work. I’ve spoken about this previously in my posts. Although I’m not specifically recommending it here, it serves as a case in point.

In this approach, you learn to view your less mature, emotional, or wounded aspects of self as the child you once were. Often, that child will have gone through some difficult times that forced him/her to learn to regulate emotions and view the world in ways that don’t serve you well in adulthood. To heal this part of ourselves, we practice seeing it as a separate entity (child). The rational/adult part of our brain then gets to serve as the caring and supportive adult caregiver who can contain and advise the more emotional and less controlled part.

5. Carefully consider how and when you will measure your progress

Sometimes when you make positive changes, the immediate result might seem negative. For example, if you quit drinking, all of your drinking buddies might get uncomfortable hanging out with you. In short, you might lose access to your old social support system and access to romantic partners if you are single. Addressing the social support issue is one of the main reasons people consider 12-step meetings. In this case, even though the short-term impact of not drinking could seem negative, the long-term impact is likely to be healthier friends and a more sustainable, healthy lifestyle.

Similarly, if you change some of your behaviors within your family system, like caretaking others, controlling, or being in the problem or “sick role,” the short-term outcome might not feel positive. Families (and work/friend systems) usually are in some sort of emotional balance (called homeostasis). When one person changes their role in the system, it throws the system out of balance, and everyone else has to adjust their behaviors or roles to accommodate the change. Some people in the system might not like the change or the disequilibrium it creates, and they may act out in an attempt to pull you back into your role. So, the short-term impact might be to feel more cut off or alienated from family members, but the long-term impact might be healthier long-term relationships that work for you.

To summarize: The suggestions I put forward in this post just touch the surface of what really would encompass a book. But I believe these are some of the most actionable principles available to get you started. And, above all, be sure to give yourself some grace and self-compassion… and this alone will do wonders to help you make change happen.

item.title: Inside the World of an Intimacy Coordinator
item.description:
Relationships

Inside the World of an Intimacy Coordinator

How actors can feel psychologically and physically safe.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Intimacy coordinators build safety before filming by discussing boundaries and securing consent.
  • Actors’ limits can reshape how directors film scenes, including how much nudity appears.
  • Simulated sex can use multiple barriers and Pilates balls to prevent direct intimate contact.

Recently, after seeing a stage play, I spoke to a lead actor about how she is able to feel safe during physically intimate scenes in front of an audience. She told me that there is an intimacy coordinator who comes onto the set to make sure the actors’ feelings about intimacy with other actors are taken into account. She has also worked on film sets with an intimacy coordinator when she felt uneasy and vulnerable in front of the camera and crew and her lover in the film.

I wanted to find out more about this and, unexpectedly, I met intimacy coordinator Christina McHugh at an event in New Mexico a few weeks later. I asked her to define what it is that she does when she is hired to work on films. “Old-fashioned doctors went house to house, a mail person goes door to door, and an intimacy coordinator goes set to set.” The geographical areas she covered were Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and movie ranches. She goes from one set to another.

She explained that making actors feel psychologically and physically safe was mostly prep work, before the scenes were shot. She had extensive conversations with directors and then worked with the actors to find out what their boundaries were and to get their consent. “Then I would go back to the director and impart information like the fact that the actor wanted less nudity. I would ask the director if it could be filmed a different way.”

For filming sex scenes, she used things like a “half-deflated Pilates ball to put between the actors’ crotches. There were often three layers of barriers between the actors for simulated sex. If the woman is on top of the man, her bouncing is done with a 9-inch Pilates ball that makes it look like simulated sex.”

McHugh said that her job entails negotiating boundaries with individual actors, the director, and trying to get all sides to agree. This is especially true in building trust on the set of a film with hyper-exposure, that includes nudity, simulated sex, and sexual violence.

Some of the sets she worked on include "Better Call Saul," "Pluribus," "Love Lies Bleeding," "Obliterated," "Duster," "The Cleaning Lady," "Waco," and "Dead for a Dollar."

I inquired where she learned her profession, and she replied that she trained with the Intimacy Professionals Association. “In about 2017, it was the first time it showed up in a credit line. It started with an HBO series, "The Deuce," which was about the porn industry. The actress felt she was being treated as a porn star and not an actress.”

I believed her when McHugh said you need a spine made of titanium to deal with producers and directors. She is not flippant about the issues actors have when she is negotiating with them. She said that young female actors tell her about being victims of sexual predation, and she takes care of them. This is an important part of her job, which she takes very seriously.

Entertainment writer Liz Konkel had this to say in a recent post on Cinema Blend: “The rules have certainly changed in regard to how sex scenes are filmed, thanks to the rise of intimacy coordinators on sets. Now, this doesn't mean we don't get plenty of steamy content. However, what it does mean is that more technical work goes into creating such scenes. In a post #MeToo Movement industry, these coordinators also help ensure actors feel comfortable and protected during intimate scenes.”

In the same article, she also addressed how actors’ boundaries and trust concerns were dealt with before intimacy coordinators. “Back in the early aughts, scenes were seemingly required of the actors if it was in the script. However, some performers have since shared stories where trust was taken advantage of on set. For instance, "Basic Instinct’s" Sharon Stone has made claims involving inappropriate requests for nudity amid production. With that, many now consider intimacy coordinators to be essential.”

item.title: Later Daters Still Love Sex
item.description:
Sex

Later Daters Still Love Sex

Sexual interest and activity in later life challenge persistent ageist myths.

Posted November 16, 2026

Key points
  • Prevalent myths about older adults becoming less sexual—or less sexually desirous—are destructive and untrue.
  • A study finds that about 1 in 4 adults ages 75–85 reported sexual contact with someone in the past year.
  • The study sampled heterosexual dating-site users, limiting conclusions about other older singles.
Source: nairi/diversify lens

Among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex. On the contrary, research shows that about three-quarters of those aged 57-64, over half of those aged 65-74, and a quarter of those aged 75-85 had sexual contact with someone in the past year. And this doesn’t even count those who would have chosen to have sex but had no opportunity.

While the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner. It’s true older adults may struggle with aspects of sex they didn’t confront when younger—men with the ability to maintain erections or ejaculate; women with lubrication or discomfort. But there are excellent treatments for these conditions, and humans are creative. Older adults engage in satisfying romantic relationships without sexual activity, satisfying sexual relationships without romance, and everything in between. And in terms of sex, older couples not only enjoy intercourse, but also non-penetrative sexual activities like hugging, cuddling, sleeping naked; manual, masturbatory, and oral play activities, and more.

A recent study by Harris and Melanson (2026) interviewed 100 single older adults aged 60-83 (50 women and 50 men) recruited from dating sites for gender, racial, and educational diversity. More older adults are single today than ever before (due to longer lives and the acceptance of divorce), and this group is understudied compared to older adults with partners. The Harris and Melanson study was limited by heterosexual participants, but we can extrapolate many of its findings to all relationships:

  • Most participants felt sex was a dealbreaker. In other words, they would not pursue a relationship with someone if sex was not a possibility. They acknowledged sex might not occur as frequently as when they were younger and may need to be adapted to aging or disabled bodies, but that was achievable. They viewed any barriers to sexual activity from having an older body as something they could adapt to.
  • Some men held myths about post-menopausal women losing interest in sex or not being able to enjoy it. But these men also considered these issues, if present, problems to be solved rather than death knells to a satisfying sexual relationship.
  • Women expected many, if not most, older men to experience erectile dysfunction, but didn’t see this as a dealbreaker. If a potential partner refused to discuss or problem-solve an issue—leaving it unresolved or avoided—that was a dealbreaker.
  • They valued quality, not quantity. Respondents generally expected sex to look different than it did (and occur less frequently) than when they were younger. This didn’t take away from the relationship importance or satisfaction around sexuality. For some, it even seemed to deepen the intimacy or excitement: if sex was less frequent, it could be savored more.

Sex is a healthy part of life throughout adulthood, whether one is single, partnered, or in between. How it looks and when it happens may change, and some adults may do well without a partner, but the majority of older adults, like younger adults, find partnered sex an important ingredient of healthy social lives, life satisfaction, and wellbeing.

Source: Jcomp/Getty Images

Harris and Melanson surveyed an often-ignored group of older adults—those who are single. Because they found them through dating sites, we know participants in the sample were at least somewhat interested in pursuing romantic and/or sexual partnerships. It’s up to future researchers to explore whether single older adults not interested in dating are equally interested in sex (with another person), or simply feel content alone; as well as how these results may be different in LGBTQ+ and other marginalized populations.

item.title: The Joy of Reading
item.description:
Education

The Joy of Reading

Why college students should read more.

Posted November 16, 2026

Source: Susan Q. Yin/ Unsplash

As a college professor for over 30 years, I have worked with countless students who either claim they hate reading or report that they've never finished an entire book. To succeed in college, it’s important to read what’s assigned. It’s also important to read for pleasure. Why? Because, simply put, it makes you more interesting.

With students nearing the end of the semester and hopefully thinking about how they can improve their habits and skills for the new semester, it is worth thinking about the role of reading. With the holiday break almost upon us, it's the perfect time to practice and to embark on a potentially interesting book.

People who read have a greater sense of fluency of ideas and perspectives that they can bring to bear on conversations, and they possess stronger vocabularies. These qualities give people an edge both socially and professionally. Referencing something you read and learned that resonates with you or naturally relates to a conversation during a job interview, for example, helps position you as someone with insight and depth.

The other thing to remember is that the habit of reading often translates to greater agility with writing. When you have more exposure to a variety of ways that ideas are expressed, you’re able to gather more information to craft what you want to say.

College is a great time to discover exactly what it is that you like to read. This is especially true if you’re coming to college with little interest in reading. This lack of interest is often due to not having had much say in what you got to read in high school. So, now’s the time to think about what you gravitate to most. What do you find most moving and compelling? Maybe it’s fiction, nonfiction, creative nonfiction, or poetry. Whatever it is, reading is a passport for the experience of world-traveling, which is a gift you can give yourself.

If your parents read to you when you were a child, they may have shown you the value and joy of reading. I’ve started directly asking my students if a parent or guardian read to or with them, what their favorite book was as a child, and what their favorite is now. What’s most sad for me is when students aren’t able to name a single book and instead tell me they “never read,” “never had a parent read to me,” “hate reading,” or “never finished a book.”

But even if the value of reading was not instilled in you growing up, it’s not too late to develop a habit of reading for pleasure. Find something that potentially interests you, put your phone away where it’s not even visible, grab a fun drink or snack, and curl up in a cozy space and read. Try just 15 minutes at first. If you like it, keep going. If you find yourself restless or sleepy, try to push through a bit longer, and if that doesn’t work then go do something else and make a commitment to yourself to return to the book the next day. Typically, those in the regular practice of reading and enjoying it generally find it easier to be alone and enjoy solitude.

In summary, when college students work to strengthen their reading muscle, both in terms of reading for classes and for pleasure, they encounter the following benefits:

  • Becoming more intriguing people
  • Building their vocabulary
  • Becoming better writers
  • Opening up new vistas on the world
  • Becoming more comfortable conversing about a range of subjects
  • Feeling more at ease by themselves
